items.stem: In a de-icing heater manifold on a weather mast, an ideal 16.5 V DC source drives a 8 Ω limiting resistor connected in series with parallel 4 Ω and 12 Ω resistors, as shown. What electrical power is dissipated in the 12 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 8 + 3.00 = 11.0 Ω. Supply current I = 16.5 / 11.0 = 1.50 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 1.50 × 3.00 = 4.50 V. Power in 12 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 12 = 1.69 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 4.50 V and calculates P = 1.69 W.

items.stem: The schematic represents a benchtop calibration rig in a physics lab supplied at 65 V with negligible internal resistance. A 11 Ω resistor lies in the main feed ahead of parallel 20 Ω and 60 Ω branches. How much thermal power is dissipated in the 20 Ω branch resistor?

markScheme.criterion: Determines parallel voltage 37.5 V and obtains 70.3 W.

items.stem: While bench-testing a dual-zone incubator heating stage, an engineer wires a 10 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 24 Ω and 48 Ω resistors across an ideal 91 V supply. What potential difference develops across the parallel 24 Ω and 48 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (24 × 48)/(24 + 48) = 16.0 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 91 × 16.0 / (10 + 16.0) = 56.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 16.0 Ω and finds V_p = 56.0 V.

items.stem: An ideal 84 V power unit energises a submersible ROV auxiliary power bus made from a 5 Ω series element followed by 45 Ω and 90 Ω resistors in parallel, as illustrated. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (45 × 90)/(45 + 90) = 30.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 5 + 30.0 = 35.0 Ω. Supply current I = 84 / 35.0 = 2.40 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 5 Ω with R_p = 30.0 Ω to obtain I = 2.40 A.

items.stem: Parallel resistors of 40 Ω and 60 Ω inside a precision optical-table thermal stabiliser receive current through a 17 Ω series resistor from an ideal 123 V cell. What electrical power is dissipated in the 60 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (40 × 60)/(40 + 60) = 24.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 17 + 24.0 = 41.0 Ω. Supply current I = 123 / 41.0 = 3.00 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 3.00 × 24.0 = 72.0 V. Power in 60 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 60 = 86.4 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 72.0 V and calculates P = 86.4 W.

items.stem: A greenhouse misting-valve controller operates from an ideal 11.2 V rail; current traverses a 6 Ω ballast resistor before splitting across 12 Ω and 24 Ω parallel arms. What potential difference develops across the parallel 12 Ω and 24 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (12 × 24)/(12 + 24) = 8.00 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 11.2 × 8.00 / (6 + 8.00) = 6.40 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 8.00 Ω and finds V_p = 6.40 V.

items.stem: Examine the circuit for a vacuum-chamber bakeout resistor assembly, where a 5 Ω resistor stands in series with parallel 30 Ω and 60 Ω branches across an ideal 37.5 V source. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (30 × 60)/(30 + 60) = 20.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 5 + 20.0 = 25.0 Ω. Supply current I = 37.5 / 25.0 = 1.50 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 5 Ω with R_p = 20.0 Ω to obtain I = 1.50 A.

items.stem: In a traction-motor dynamic braking test bank, an ideal 38.4 V DC source drives a 6 Ω limiting resistor connected in series with parallel 14 Ω and 35 Ω resistors, as shown. What electrical power is dissipated in the 35 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (14 × 35)/(14 + 35) = 10.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 6 + 10.0 = 16.0 Ω. Supply current I = 38.4 / 16.0 = 2.40 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 2.40 × 10.0 = 24.0 V. Power in 35 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 35 = 16.5 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 24.0 V and calculates P = 16.5 W.

items.stem: While bench-testing a balloon telemetry heater loop, an engineer wires a 18 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 15 Ω and 60 Ω resistors across an ideal 60 V supply. What potential difference develops across the parallel 15 Ω and 60 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (15 × 60)/(15 + 60) = 12.0 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 60 × 12.0 / (18 + 12.0) = 24.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 12.0 Ω and finds V_p = 24.0 V.

items.stem: An ideal 40 V power unit energises an industrial kiln damper actuator network made from a 15 Ω series element followed by 15 Ω and 30 Ω resistors in parallel, as illustrated. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (15 × 30)/(15 + 30) = 10.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 15 + 10.0 = 25.0 Ω. Supply current I = 40 / 25.0 = 1.60 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 15 Ω with R_p = 10.0 Ω to obtain I = 1.60 A.

items.stem: Parallel resistors of 45 Ω and 90 Ω inside a cryogenic transfer-line warm-up harness receive current through a 8 Ω series resistor from an ideal 45.6 V cell. What electrical power is dissipated in the 90 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (45 × 90)/(45 + 90) = 30.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 8 + 30.0 = 38.0 Ω. Supply current I = 45.6 / 38.0 = 1.20 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 1.20 × 30.0 = 36.0 V. Power in 90 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 90 = 14.4 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 36.0 V and calculates P = 14.4 W.

items.stem: To regulate heating in a cleanroom airlock interlock load bank, engineers connect parallel 18 Ω and 36 Ω resistors in series with a 10 Ω drop resistor across an ideal 52.8 V source.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 12.0 Ω and adds 10 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 22.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 2.40 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 28.8 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 36.
Obtains P = 23.0 W.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a marine radar waveguide dryer circuit: an ideal 48 V source drives a 6 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 15 Ω and 30 Ω resistors.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 10.0 Ω and adds 6 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 16.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 3.00 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 30.0 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 15.
Obtains P = 60.0 W.

items.stem: A battery-cycler dummy load module uses an ideal 30 V DC supply connected to a 3 Ω series resistor and a parallel combination of 15 Ω and 60 Ω resistors, as shown.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 12.0 Ω and adds 3 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 15.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 2.00 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 24.0 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 60.
Obtains P = 9.60 W.

items.stem: The diagram illustrates a laser chiller bypass resistor network powered by an ideal 82 V source; current passes through a 17 Ω resistor before dividing between parallel 40 Ω and 60 Ω branches.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 24.0 Ω and adds 17 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 41.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 2.00 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 48.0 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 40.
Obtains P = 57.6 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 15.0 Ω and adds 16 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 31.0 Ω.

Obtains V_p = 52.5 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 60.
Obtains P = 45.9 W.

items.stem: During commissioning of a microplate reader warm-up stage, an ideal 84 V supply feeds a 12 Ω main-branch resistor followed by parallel 18 Ω and 36 Ω resistive loads.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 12.0 Ω and adds 12 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 24.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 3.50 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 42.0 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 18.

items.stem: The resistive network of a geothermal logger downhole heater places 10 Ω and 15 Ω elements in parallel, fed via a 9 Ω series ballast from an ideal 45 V cell.

items.stem: An ideal 12 V DC supply powers an air-quality sensor manifold with two parallel paths, as shown: one path holds 13 Ω and 17 Ω resistors in series, while the second holds a 28 Ω resistor. What current is registered by the ideal ammeter A?
items.workedSolution: Composite branch resistance = 13 + 17 = 30 Ω, so I_1 = 12 / 30 = 0.400 A. Parallel branch current I_2 = 12 / 28 = 0.429 A. By Kirchhoff's junction rule, ammeter reading I_tot = I_1 + I_2 = 0.829 A.

markScheme.criterion: Sums branch currents 0.400 A and 0.429 A to obtain 0.829 A.

items.stem: In a dashboard indicator harness, an ideal 37.4 V supply feeds a 11 Ω series resistor connected to three parallel branches of 30 Ω, 20 Ω, and 12 Ω, as shown. What current flows through the 30 Ω branch?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/30 + 1/20 + 1/12, giving R_p = 6.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 11 + 6.00 = 17.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 37.4 / 17.0 = 2.20 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 13.2 V, and I(30 Ω) = V_p / 30 = 0.440 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 0.440 A.

items.stem: In the cleanroom fan-status monitor shown, ideal ammeter A measures the main current leaving an ideal 29 V cell before a junction splits into a 12 Ω + 7 Ω series arm and a parallel 27 Ω arm. What reading appears on ammeter A?
items.workedSolution: Composite branch resistance = 12 + 7 = 19 Ω, so I_1 = 29 / 19 = 1.53 A. Parallel branch current I_2 = 29 / 27 = 1.07 A. By Kirchhoff's junction rule, ammeter reading I_tot = I_1 + I_2 = 2.60 A.

markScheme.criterion: Sums branch currents 1.53 A and 1.07 A to obtain 2.60 A.

items.stem: Three resistors of 14 Ω, 21 Ω, and 42 Ω are wired in parallel inside a marine navigation beacon board and fed through a 5 Ω resistor from an ideal 36 V DC source. What is the equivalent resistance of the three-branch parallel section (14 Ω, 21 Ω, and 42 Ω)?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/14 + 1/21 + 1/42, giving R_p = 7.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 5 + 7.00 = 12.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 36 / 12.0 = 3.00 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 21.0 V, and I(14 Ω) = V_p / 14 = 1.50 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 7.00 Ω.

items.stem: A technician wires an ideal 9 V source across a railway signalling relay rack where branch X has 15 Ω and 14 Ω in series and branch Y has a 13 Ω resistor in parallel. Determine the current through ideal ammeter A in the supply line.
items.workedSolution: Composite branch resistance = 15 + 14 = 29 Ω, so I_1 = 9 / 29 = 0.310 A. Parallel branch current I_2 = 9 / 13 = 0.692 A. By Kirchhoff's junction rule, ammeter reading I_tot = I_1 + I_2 = 1.00 A.

markScheme.criterion: Sums branch currents 0.310 A and 0.692 A to obtain 1.00 A.

items.stem: The schematic for a solar observatory actuator bus shows an ideal 47.6 V cell driving a 4 Ω main-branch resistor that splits at a junction into 20 Ω, 30 Ω, and 60 Ω parallel resistors. What current flows through the 20 Ω branch?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/20 + 1/30 + 1/60, giving R_p = 10.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 4 + 10.0 = 14.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 47.6 / 14.0 = 3.40 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 34.0 V, and I(20 Ω) = V_p / 20 = 1.70 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 1.70 A.

items.stem: The schematic of a Wheatstone reference header features an ideal 15 V cell and an ideal ammeter A feeding a 8 Ω branch in parallel with a series pair of 7 Ω and 7 Ω resistors. Calculate the ammeter reading.
items.workedSolution: Composite branch resistance = 7 + 7 = 14 Ω, so I_1 = 15 / 14 = 1.07 A. Parallel branch current I_2 = 15 / 8 = 1.88 A. By Kirchhoff's junction rule, ammeter reading I_tot = I_1 + I_2 = 2.95 A.

markScheme.criterion: Sums branch currents 1.07 A and 1.88 A to obtain 2.95 A.

items.stem: Across a cryostat multi-channel heater block, a 2 Ω line resistor links an ideal 40.8 V rail to a three-way parallel manifold of 20 Ω, 30 Ω, and 60 Ω loads. What is the equivalent resistance of the three-branch parallel section (20 Ω, 30 Ω, and 60 Ω)?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/20 + 1/30 + 1/60, giving R_p = 10.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 2 + 10.0 = 12.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 40.8 / 12.0 = 3.40 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 34.0 V, and I(20 Ω) = V_p / 20 = 1.70 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 10.0 Ω.

items.stem: Two parallel branches inside a titration pump manifold—one comprising 14 Ω and 7 Ω in series, the other a single 9 Ω resistor—draw current from an ideal 28 V rail through ideal ammeter A. What does A read?
items.workedSolution: Composite branch resistance = 14 + 7 = 21 Ω, so I_1 = 28 / 21 = 1.33 A. Parallel branch current I_2 = 28 / 9 = 3.11 A. By Kirchhoff's junction rule, ammeter reading I_tot = I_1 + I_2 = 4.44 A.

markScheme.criterion: Sums branch currents 1.33 A and 3.11 A to obtain 4.44 A.

items.stem: Current from an ideal 52.8 V supply enters an avionics redundant bus monitor via a 12 Ω series resistor before dividing across 40 Ω, 60 Ω, and 24 Ω parallel elements. What current flows through the 40 Ω branch?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/40 + 1/60 + 1/24, giving R_p = 12.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 12 + 12.0 = 24.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 52.8 / 24.0 = 2.20 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 26.4 V, and I(40 Ω) = V_p / 40 = 0.660 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 0.660 A.

items.stem: An ideal 8 V DC supply powers a greenhouse louver motor array with two parallel paths, as shown: one path holds 15 Ω and 18 Ω resistors in series, while the second holds a 13 Ω resistor. What current is registered by the ideal ammeter A?
items.workedSolution: Composite branch resistance = 15 + 18 = 33 Ω, so I_1 = 8 / 33 = 0.242 A. Parallel branch current I_2 = 8 / 13 = 0.615 A. By Kirchhoff's junction rule, ammeter reading I_tot = I_1 + I_2 = 0.858 A.

markScheme.criterion: Sums branch currents 0.242 A and 0.615 A to obtain 0.858 A.

items.stem: In a subsea valve solenoid header, an ideal 14 V supply feeds a 4 Ω series resistor connected to three parallel branches of 18 Ω, 36 Ω, and 12 Ω, as shown. What is the equivalent resistance of the three-branch parallel section (18 Ω, 36 Ω, and 12 Ω)?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/18 + 1/36 + 1/12, giving R_p = 6.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 4 + 6.00 = 10.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 14 / 10.0 = 1.40 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 8.40 V, and I(18 Ω) = V_p / 18 = 0.467 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 6.00 Ω.

items.stem: In the elevated-tank level-indicator board shown, ideal ammeter A measures the main current leaving an ideal 35 V cell before a junction splits into a 3 Ω + 13 Ω series arm and a parallel 9 Ω arm. What reading appears on ammeter A?
items.workedSolution: Composite branch resistance = 3 + 13 = 16 Ω, so I_1 = 35 / 16 = 2.19 A. Parallel branch current I_2 = 35 / 9 = 3.89 A. By Kirchhoff's junction rule, ammeter reading I_tot = I_1 + I_2 = 6.08 A.

markScheme.criterion: Sums branch currents 2.19 A and 3.89 A to obtain 6.08 A.

items.stem: Three resistors of 15 Ω, 10 Ω, and 6 Ω are wired in parallel inside an automated packaging-line sensor bus and fed through a 12 Ω resistor from an ideal 45 V DC source. What current flows through the 15 Ω branch?
items.workedSolution: 1/R_p = 1/15 + 1/10 + 1/6, giving R_p = 3.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 12 + 3.00 = 15.0 Ω. Main current I_tot = 45 / 15.0 = 3.00 A, parallel p.d. V_p = 9.00 V, and I(15 Ω) = V_p / 15 = 0.600 A.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 0.600 A.

items.stem: Engineers testing a fermenter sparger control header wire 20 Ω, 30 Ω, and 60 Ω branches in parallel and connect the group in series with a 2 Ω resistor across an ideal 31.2 V supply.

items.stem: Three parallel resistive loads (14 Ω, 21 Ω, and 42 Ω) in a seismic vault telemetry distribution hub draw power through a 6 Ω line resistor from an ideal 23.4 V cell.

markScheme.criterion: Applies 1/R_p = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3 and inverts.
Obtains R_p = 7.00 Ω.
Adds 6 Ω to R_p and uses I = V / R_tot.
Obtains I_tot = 1.80 A.
Calculates V_p = 12.6 V and divides by 14 Ω.
Obtains I_1 = 0.900 A.

items.stem: In a rechargeable battery trickle-charging loop (shown by its equivalent source ε and internal resistance r), two cells of emf 20 V (internal resistance 0.8 Ω) and 9 V (internal resistance 1.1 Ω) are wired in opposition—positive to positive—with 7 Ω and 10 Ω series resistors. What steady current circulates around the loop?
items.workedSolution: By Kirchhoff's loop law, net emf ε_net = 20 − 9 = 11 V, while all series resistances add: R_tot = 0.8 + 1.1 + 7 + 10 = 18.9 Ω. Loop current I = 11 / 18.9 = 0.582 A. Load p.d. V = 5.82 V and load power P = 3.39 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's loop law with opposing emfs and summed internal resistances to obtain 0.582 A.

items.stem: Testing Kirchhoff's loop rule on an emergency backup DC bus tie circuit, a student connects a 9 V cell (1.8 Ω internal resistance) against an opposing 4 V cell (1.3 Ω internal resistance) through 7 Ω and 11 Ω external resistors (equivalent ε, r illustrated). markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's loop law with opposing emfs and summed internal resistances to obtain 0.618 W.

items.stem: Within a portable solar-cell battery float charger, positive terminals of a 14 V cell (1.8 Ω) and a 6 V cell (1.5 Ω) are joined so their emfs oppose around a single loop (equivalent ε, r shown) containing 4 Ω and 15 Ω resistors. What is the potential difference across the 15 Ω load resistor?
items.workedSolution: By Kirchhoff's loop law, net emf ε_net = 14 − 6 = 8 V, while all series resistances add: R_tot = 1.8 + 1.5 + 4 + 15 = 22.3 Ω. Loop current I = 8 / 22.3 = 0.359 A. Load p.d. V = 5.38 V and load power P = 1.93 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kirchhoff's loop law with opposing emfs and summed internal resistances to obtain 5.38 V.

items.stem: A single-loop reversible electrochemistry cell comparison rig combines opposing sources (19 V with 1.8 Ω, and 6 V with 1.3 Ω; depicted as net ε and r) in series with 7 Ω and 10 Ω resistive elements. What thermal power is dissipated in the 10 Ω load resistor?

items.stem: Refer to the equivalent loop for a dual-battery jump-start bench: a 9 V battery (1.6 Ω internal resistance) charges an opposing 4 V battery (0.9 Ω internal resistance) via 3 Ω and 8 Ω series resistors. What steady current circulates around the loop?

items.stem: On an analogue moving-coil meter bench, resistors of 140 Ω and 160 Ω form a series divider across an ideal 35 V DC supply. A finite-resistance voltmeter (480 Ω, drawn as the parallel branch) is placed across the 160 Ω resistor. What reading does the voltmeter show?
items.workedSolution: The 480 Ω voltmeter shunts the 160 Ω resistor: R_p = (160 × 480)/(160 + 480) = 120 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 35 × 120 / (140 + 120) = 16.2 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 160 Ω and 480 Ω in parallel (120 Ω) to obtain V = 16.2 V.

items.stem: A series divider in a high-impedance sensor divider jig has a 100 Ω upper arm and 900 Ω lower arm across an ideal 36 V source. Connecting a non-ideal 1800 Ω voltmeter across the 900 Ω arm (forming the parallel pair shown) yields what potential difference?
items.workedSolution: The 1800 Ω voltmeter shunts the 900 Ω resistor: R_p = (900 × 1800)/(900 + 1800) = 600 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 36 × 600 / (100 + 600) = 30.9 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 900 Ω and 1800 Ω in parallel (600 Ω) to obtain V = 30.9 V.

items.stem: In a physics teaching potentiometer station, a non-ideal moving-coil ammeter of coil resistance 3.6 Ω (modelled as the 3.6 Ω series element) sits in the main line of an ideal 8 V source feeding parallel 4 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. What current does the ammeter register?
items.workedSolution: Parallel load R_p = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3.00 Ω. Including the non-ideal ammeter resistance 3.6 Ω gives R_tot = 3.6 + 3.00 = 6.60 Ω, so I = 8 / 6.60 = 1.21 A.

markScheme.criterion: Includes ammeter coil resistance 3.6 Ω in series with R_p = 3.00 Ω to obtain 1.21 A.

items.stem: In the galvanometer multiplier test rig schematic, the 2400 Ω parallel element represents a voltmeter shunting the 1200 Ω lower resistor of a divider fed through 750 Ω from an ideal 10 V cell. Calculate the voltmeter reading.
items.workedSolution: The 2400 Ω voltmeter shunts the 1200 Ω resistor: R_p = (1200 × 2400)/(1200 + 2400) = 800 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 10 × 800 / (750 + 800) = 5.16 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 1200 Ω and 2400 Ω in parallel (800 Ω) to obtain V = 5.16 V.

items.stem: An ideal 15 V rail energises an industrial PLC input-impedance check with 130 Ω and 200 Ω series resistors; probing across 200 Ω with a 300 Ω finite-impedance voltmeter (shown in parallel) produces what reading?
items.workedSolution: The 300 Ω voltmeter shunts the 200 Ω resistor: R_p = (200 × 300)/(200 + 300) = 120 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 15 × 120 / (130 + 120) = 7.20 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 200 Ω and 300 Ω in parallel (120 Ω) to obtain V = 7.20 V.

items.stem: A technician inserts an ammeter with internal resistance 2 Ω (drawn as the 2 Ω series resistor) between an ideal 23 V rail and parallel 4 Ω and 12 Ω loads on an ECG electrode-bias divider stage. Determine the ammeter reading.
items.workedSolution: Parallel load R_p = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3.00 Ω. Including the non-ideal ammeter resistance 2 Ω gives R_tot = 2 + 3.00 = 5.00 Ω, so I = 23 / 5.00 = 4.60 A.

markScheme.criterion: Includes ammeter coil resistance 2 Ω in series with R_p = 3.00 Ω to obtain 4.60 A.

items.stem: On a photodiode bias divider network, resistors of 225 Ω and 350 Ω form a series divider across an ideal 34 V DC supply. A finite-resistance voltmeter (875 Ω, drawn as the parallel branch) is placed across the 350 Ω resistor. What reading does the voltmeter show?
items.workedSolution: The 875 Ω voltmeter shunts the 350 Ω resistor: R_p = (350 × 875)/(350 + 875) = 250 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 34 × 250 / (225 + 250) = 17.9 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 350 Ω and 875 Ω in parallel (250 Ω) to obtain V = 17.9 V.

items.stem: A series divider in an automotive harness diagnostic probe has a 750 Ω upper arm and 2000 Ω lower arm across an ideal 18 V source. Connecting a non-ideal 3000 Ω voltmeter across the 2000 Ω arm (forming the parallel pair shown) yields what potential difference?
items.workedSolution: The 3000 Ω voltmeter shunts the 2000 Ω resistor: R_p = (2000 × 3000)/(2000 + 3000) = 1.20 × 10³ Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 18 × 1.20 × 10³ / (750 + 1.20 × 10³) = 11.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 2000 Ω and 3000 Ω in parallel (1.20 × 10³ Ω) to obtain V = 11.1 V.

items.stem: When a 1.6 Ω non-ideal ammeter (shown in series) measures the supply current to 20 Ω and 60 Ω parallel branches across an ideal 29 V cell in a vacuum-tube grid-bias divider check, what current flows?
items.workedSolution: Parallel load R_p = (20 × 60)/(20 + 60) = 15.0 Ω. Including the non-ideal ammeter resistance 1.6 Ω gives R_tot = 1.6 + 15.0 = 16.6 Ω, so I = 29 / 16.6 = 1.75 A.

markScheme.criterion: Includes ammeter coil resistance 1.6 Ω in series with R_p = 15.0 Ω to obtain 1.75 A.

items.stem: In the piezo-amplifier bias test point schematic, the 1200 Ω parallel element represents a voltmeter shunting the 800 Ω lower resistor of a divider fed through 260 Ω from an ideal 42 V cell. Calculate the voltmeter reading.
items.workedSolution: The 1200 Ω voltmeter shunts the 800 Ω resistor: R_p = (800 × 1200)/(800 + 1200) = 480 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 42 × 480 / (260 + 480) = 27.2 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 800 Ω and 1200 Ω in parallel (480 Ω) to obtain V = 27.2 V.

items.stem: An ideal 38 V rail energises a pH-probe reference divider bench with 250 Ω and 525 Ω series resistors; probing across 525 Ω with a 700 Ω finite-impedance voltmeter (shown in parallel) produces what reading?
items.workedSolution: The 700 Ω voltmeter shunts the 525 Ω resistor: R_p = (525 × 700)/(525 + 700) = 300 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 38 × 300 / (250 + 300) = 20.7 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 525 Ω and 700 Ω in parallel (300 Ω) to obtain V = 20.7 V.

items.stem: In a radiation-detector HV bleed divider, a non-ideal moving-coil ammeter of coil resistance 3.2 Ω (modelled as the 3.2 Ω series element) sits in the main line of an ideal 10 V source feeding parallel 9 Ω and 18 Ω resistors. What current does the ammeter register?
items.workedSolution: Parallel load R_p = (9 × 18)/(9 + 18) = 6.00 Ω. Including the non-ideal ammeter resistance 3.2 Ω gives R_tot = 3.2 + 6.00 = 9.20 Ω, so I = 10 / 9.20 = 1.09 A.

markScheme.criterion: Includes ammeter coil resistance 3.2 Ω in series with R_p = 6.00 Ω to obtain 1.09 A.

items.stem: On a strain-bridge balance verification rig, resistors of 30 Ω and 180 Ω form a series divider across an ideal 34 V DC supply. A finite-resistance voltmeter (90 Ω, drawn as the parallel branch) is placed across the 180 Ω resistor. What reading does the voltmeter show?
items.workedSolution: The 90 Ω voltmeter shunts the 180 Ω resistor: R_p = (180 × 90)/(180 + 90) = 60.0 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 34 × 60.0 / (30 + 60.0) = 22.7 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 180 Ω and 90 Ω in parallel (60.0 Ω) to obtain V = 22.7 V.

items.stem: A series divider in an audio preamp bias-point check has a 120 Ω upper arm and 400 Ω lower arm across an ideal 45 V source. Connecting a non-ideal 1200 Ω voltmeter across the 400 Ω arm (forming the parallel pair shown) yields what potential difference?
items.workedSolution: The 1200 Ω voltmeter shunts the 400 Ω resistor: R_p = (400 × 1200)/(400 + 1200) = 300 Ω. Loaded voltmeter reading V_out = 45 × 300 / (120 + 300) = 32.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 400 Ω and 1200 Ω in parallel (300 Ω) to obtain V = 32.1 V.

items.stem: A technician inserts an ammeter with internal resistance 2.4 Ω (drawn as the 2.4 Ω series resistor) between an ideal 19 V rail and parallel 36 Ω and 12 Ω loads on a solar-cell shunt-meter test bench. Determine the ammeter reading.
items.workedSolution: Parallel load R_p = (36 × 12)/(36 + 12) = 9.00 Ω. Including the non-ideal ammeter resistance 2.4 Ω gives R_tot = 2.4 + 9.00 = 11.4 Ω, so I = 19 / 11.4 = 1.67 A.

markScheme.criterion: Includes ammeter coil resistance 2.4 Ω in series with R_p = 9.00 Ω to obtain 1.67 A.

items.stem: An automatic street-lamp twilight switch uses an ideal 15 V DC supply, an LDR, and a 15 kΩ fixed resistor wired as shown, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. The LDR resistance is 129 kΩ in darkness and 1 kΩ in bright light. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 129 + 15 = 144 kΩ, so I_dark = 15 / 144000 = 1.04 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 1.56 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 15 × 15 / (1 + 15) = 14.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 15 kΩ resistor to obtain 14.1 V.

items.stem: In the greenhouse shade-curtain controller diagram, an LDR (47 kΩ dark; 2.5 kΩ bright) sits in series with a 3 kΩ resistor across an ideal 12 V cell while ideal voltmeter Vout monitors the 3 kΩ resistor. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 47 + 3 = 50 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 50000 = 2.40 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.720 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 3 / (2.5 + 3) = 6.55 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 3 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.720 V.

items.stem: Testing a museum light-exposure alarm circuit supplied at 9 V (ideal), illumination lowers the LDR resistance from 124 kΩ in darkness to 2.5 kΩ in bright light; Vout is measured across the series 2 kΩ resistor. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 124 + 2 = 126 kΩ, so I_dark = 9 / 126000 = 7.14 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.143 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 9 × 2 / (2.5 + 2) = 4.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 2 kΩ resistor to obtain 7.14 × 10⁻⁵ A.

items.stem: The sensing stage of a photographic darkroom door interlock connects an LDR (153 kΩ in darkness, 3.5 kΩ when brightly lit) and a 15 kΩ resistor across an ideal 12 V source, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 153 + 15 = 168 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 168000 = 7.14 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 1.07 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 15 / (3.5 + 15) = 9.73 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 15 kΩ resistor to obtain 9.73 V.

items.stem: An ideal 9 V rail powers a solar tracker dusk-detection stage comprising an LDR (43 kΩ dark, 2.5 kΩ bright) in series with a 5 kΩ output resistor bridged by ideal voltmeter Vout. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 43 + 5 = 48 kΩ, so I_dark = 9 / 48000 = 1.88 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.938 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 9 × 5 / (2.5 + 5) = 6.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 5 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.938 V.

items.stem: Within a poultry-house lighting relay, an ideal voltmeter Vout spans a 20 kΩ resistor in series with an LDR (28 kΩ in darkness; 1.2 kΩ in bright daylight) across an ideal 15 V supply. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 28 + 20 = 48 kΩ, so I_dark = 15 / 48000 = 3.13 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 6.25 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 15 × 20 / (1.2 + 20) = 14.2 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 3.13 × 10⁻⁴ A.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a warehouse skylight dimming sensor: an LDR whose resistance changes between 51 kΩ (dark) and 1.5 kΩ (bright) forms a divider with a 8 kΩ resistor across 24 V (ideal). What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 51 + 8 = 59 kΩ, so I_dark = 24 / 59000 = 4.07 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 3.25 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 24 × 8 / (1.5 + 8) = 20.2 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 8 kΩ resistor to obtain 20.2 V.

items.stem: A conveyor-belt optical package counter uses an ideal 18 V DC supply, an LDR, and a 20 kΩ fixed resistor wired as shown, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. The LDR resistance is 89 kΩ in darkness and 0.8 kΩ in bright light. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 89 + 20 = 109 kΩ, so I_dark = 18 / 109000 = 1.65 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 3.30 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 18 × 20 / (0.8 + 20) = 17.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 3.30 V.

items.stem: In the observatory dome-shutter safety sensor diagram, an LDR (175 kΩ dark; 0.5 kΩ bright) sits in series with a 12 kΩ resistor across an ideal 5 V cell while ideal voltmeter Vout monitors the 12 kΩ resistor. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 175 + 12 = 187 kΩ, so I_dark = 5 / 187000 = 2.67 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.321 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 5 × 12 / (0.5 + 12) = 4.80 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 12 kΩ resistor to obtain 2.67 × 10⁻⁵ A.

items.stem: Testing a meteorological sunshine-duration logger supplied at 12 V (ideal), illumination lowers the LDR resistance from 151 kΩ in darkness to 3.5 kΩ in bright light; Vout is measured across the series 3 kΩ resistor. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 151 + 3 = 154 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 154000 = 7.79 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.234 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 3 / (3.5 + 3) = 5.54 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 3 kΩ resistor to obtain 5.54 V.

items.stem: The sensing stage of a stairwell dusk-to-dawn LED trigger connects an LDR (109 kΩ in darkness, 2.5 kΩ when brightly lit) and a 15 kΩ resistor across an ideal 12 V source, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 109 + 15 = 124 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 124000 = 9.68 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 1.45 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 15 / (2.5 + 15) = 10.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 15 kΩ resistor to obtain 1.45 V.

items.stem: An ideal 9 V rail powers a highway tunnel entrance luminance monitor comprising an LDR (65 kΩ dark, 0.8 kΩ bright) in series with a 20 kΩ output resistor bridged by ideal voltmeter Vout. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 65 + 20 = 85 kΩ, so I_dark = 9 / 85000 = 1.06 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 2.12 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 9 × 20 / (0.8 + 20) = 8.65 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 1.06 × 10⁻⁴ A.

items.stem: Within an aquarium photoperiod timer sensor, an ideal voltmeter Vout spans a 2 kΩ resistor in series with an LDR (45 kΩ in darkness; 2.5 kΩ in bright daylight) across an ideal 6 V supply. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 45 + 2 = 47 kΩ, so I_dark = 6 / 47000 = 1.28 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.255 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 6 × 2 / (2.5 + 2) = 2.67 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 2 kΩ resistor to obtain 2.67 V.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a railway level-crossing beacon dimmer: an LDR whose resistance changes between 180 kΩ (dark) and 1.5 kΩ (bright) forms a divider with a 10 kΩ resistor across 24 V (ideal). What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 10 kΩ resistor to obtain 1.26 V.

items.stem: Across an ideal 18 V DC terminal pair in an automated venetian-blind lux sensor, an LDR of dark resistance 44 kΩ and bright-light resistance 2.5 kΩ sits in series with a 10 kΩ resistor spanned by ideal voltmeter Vout.

markScheme.criterion: Converts kΩ to Ω and sums 44 kΩ + 10 kΩ.
Obtains I_dark = 3.33 × 10⁻⁴ A.
Multiplies I_dark by R_fixed or applies divider formula.
Obtains V_out(dark) = 3.33 V.
Uses bright LDR resistance 2.5 kΩ in potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_out(bright) = 14.4 V.

items.stem: In a neonatal incubator thermal-alarm divider, an NTC thermistor (resistance decreases as temperature rises) has resistance 500 Ω at the operating point and sits in series with a 380 Ω fixed resistor across an ideal 24 V DC supply, as shown. What potential difference appears across the 500 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 380 + 500 = 880 Ω. Current I = 24 / 880 = 0.0273 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 24 × 500 / 880 = 13.6 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.372 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 13.6 V.

items.stem: An NTC thermistor R_1 (resistance decreases with rising temperature) sits in series with a 400 Ω resistor across an ideal 24 V source in a lithium-ion pack over-temperature cutoff, as shown. When an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 14.0 V, what is the resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 400 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 24 − 14.0 = 10.0 V. Current I = 10.0 / 400 = 0.0250 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 14.0 / 0.0250 = 560 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 10.0 V to find I = 0.0250 A and R_1 = 560 Ω.

items.stem: The divider stage of an engine-coolant sensing bridge wires a 560 Ω reference resistor in series with an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient; 660 Ω at the test temperature) across an ideal 24 V source. What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 660 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 560 + 660 = 1220 Ω. Current I = 24 / 1220 = 0.0197 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 24 × 660 / 1220 = 13.0 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.255 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.255 W.

items.stem: In the 3D-printer hot-end thermistor loop diagram, R_1 is an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) wired in series with a 440 Ω precision resistor across an ideal 33 V supply. At an operating point where the p.d. across R_1 is 21.0 V, calculate R_1.
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 440 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 33 − 21.0 = 12.0 V. Current I = 12.0 / 440 = 0.0273 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 21.0 / 0.0273 = 770 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 12.0 V to find I = 0.0273 A and R_1 = 770 Ω.

items.stem: During steady-state calibration of a fermentation vat temperature regulator, an ideal 9 V cell drives a 460 Ω resistor in series with a 660 Ω NTC thermistor (whose resistance falls with increasing temperature). What potential difference appears across the 660 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 460 + 660 = 1120 Ω. Current I = 9 / 1120 = 8.04 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 9 × 660 / 1120 = 5.30 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0426 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 5.30 V.

items.stem: Monitoring a quartz-crystal oven controller driven by an ideal 9 V cell, a technician records 6.00 V on an ideal voltmeter across NTC thermistor R_1 (whose resistance drops when warmed) in series with 570 Ω. What is R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 570 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 9 − 6.00 = 3.00 V. Current I = 3.00 / 570 = 5.26 × 10⁻³ A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 6.00 / 5.26 × 10⁻³ = 1.14 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 3.00 V to find I = 5.26 × 10⁻³ A and R_1 = 1.14 × 10³ Ω.

items.stem: Within a vaccine cold-chain data-logger probe, a 600 Ω resistor and an NTC thermistor R_1 (negative temperature coefficient) share an ideal 24 V rail; given 14.0 V across R_1, find R_1's resistance.
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 600 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 24 − 14.0 = 10.0 V. Current I = 10.0 / 600 = 0.0167 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 14.0 / 0.0167 = 840 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 10.0 V to find I = 0.0167 A and R_1 = 840 Ω.

items.stem: In a server-blade heatsink thermal monitor, an NTC thermistor (resistance decreases as temperature rises) has resistance 1090 Ω at the operating point and sits in series with a 460 Ω fixed resistor across an ideal 24 V DC supply, as shown. What potential difference appears across the 1090 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 460 + 1090 = 1550 Ω. Current I = 24 / 1550 = 0.0155 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 24 × 1090 / 1550 = 16.9 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.261 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 16.9 V.

items.stem: An NTC thermistor R_1 (resistance decreases with rising temperature) sits in series with a 540 Ω resistor across an ideal 27 V source in a water-bath thermostat calibration circuit, as shown. When an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 18.0 V, what is the resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 540 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 27 − 18.0 = 9.00 V. Current I = 9.00 / 540 = 0.0167 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 18.0 / 0.0167 = 1.08 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 9.00 V to find I = 0.0167 A and R_1 = 1.08 × 10³ Ω.

items.stem: The divider stage of a PCR thermal-cycler block sensor wires a 330 Ω reference resistor in series with an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient; 770 Ω at the test temperature) across an ideal 24 V source. What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 770 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 330 + 770 = 1100 Ω. Current I = 24 / 1100 = 0.0218 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 24 × 770 / 1100 = 16.8 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.367 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.367 W.

items.stem: In the induction-cooktop pan-temperature sensor diagram, R_1 is an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) wired in series with a 480 Ω precision resistor across an ideal 7 V supply. At an operating point where the p.d. across R_1 is 3.00 V, calculate R_1.

items.stem: An ideal 24 V rail powers a blood-warmer safety cutoff divider containing a 230 Ω series resistor and an NTC thermistor (resistance 270 Ω, decreasing when heated). What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 270 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 230 + 270 = 500 Ω. Current I = 24 / 500 = 0.0480 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 24 × 270 / 500 = 13.0 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.622 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.622 W.

items.stem: In an HVAC supply-duct air-temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor R_1 (negative temperature coefficient: resistance decreases as temperature increases) is wired in series with a 300 Ω resistor across an ideal 12 V DC source, as shown. At the test temperature, an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 7.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts 7.00 V from 12 V to find p.d. across 300 Ω.
Obtains I = 0.0167 A.
Divides V_NTC by the series current from (a).
Obtains R_1 = 420 Ω.
Uses P = V I or I² R_1.
Obtains P = 0.117 W.

items.stem: A potentiometer tap driving an actuator coil uses 3 Ω and 24 Ω divider resistors across an ideal 20 V DC source, with a 48 Ω external load wired in parallel across the 24 Ω arm as shown. What loaded output potential difference appears across the 48 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (24 × 48)/(24 + 48) = 16.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 20 × 16.0 / (3 + 16.0) = 16.8 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 48 = 0.351 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 48 = 5.91 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (16.0 Ω) to obtain 16.8 V.

items.stem: In the audio attenuator pad feeding a transducer schematic, a 8 Ω–18 Ω potential divider across 34 V (ideal) is shunted across its 18 Ω lower arm by a 36 Ω load resistor. What electrical power is delivered to the 36 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (18 × 36)/(18 + 36) = 12.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 34 × 12.0 / (8 + 12.0) = 20.4 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 36 = 0.567 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 36 = 11.6 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (12.0 Ω) to obtain 11.6 W.

items.stem: Connecting a 45 Ω resistive load across the 90 Ω lower section of a 40 Ω–90 Ω divider in a strain-gauge half-bridge feeding an ADC input supplied at 31 V (ideal) pulls down the output p.d. What current flows through the 45 Ω load branch?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (90 × 45)/(90 + 45) = 30.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 31 × 30.0 / (40 + 30.0) = 13.3 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 45 = 0.295 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 45 = 3.92 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (30.0 Ω) to obtain 0.295 A.

items.stem: An ideal 10 V cell powers an industrial proportional-valve divider stage where upper resistor 60 Ω feeds the parallel combination of lower divider arm 180 Ω and load 360 Ω. What loaded output potential difference appears across the 360 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (180 × 360)/(180 + 360) = 120 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 10 × 120 / (60 + 120) = 6.67 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 360 = 0.0185 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 360 = 0.123 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (120 Ω) to obtain 6.67 V.

items.stem: Within a thermocouple reference-bias divider, a 35 Ω load bridges the 14 Ω resistor of a series divider completed by a 4 Ω resistor across an ideal 21 V rail. What electrical power is delivered to the 35 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (14 × 35)/(14 + 35) = 10.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 21 × 10.0 / (4 + 10.0) = 15.0 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 35 = 0.429 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 35 = 6.43 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (10.0 Ω) to obtain 6.43 W.

items.stem: A laser-diode bias network with shunt load uses 10 Ω and 28 Ω divider resistors across an ideal 32 V DC source, with a 70 Ω external load wired in parallel across the 28 Ω arm as shown. What current flows through the 70 Ω load branch?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (28 × 70)/(28 + 70) = 20.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 32 × 20.0 / (10 + 20.0) = 21.3 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 70 = 0.305 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 70 = 6.50 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (20.0 Ω) to obtain 0.305 A.

items.stem: In the servo-potentiometer feedback stage schematic, a 15 Ω–20 Ω potential divider across 32 V (ideal) is shunted across its 20 Ω lower arm by a 60 Ω load resistor. What loaded output potential difference appears across the 60 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (20 × 60)/(20 + 60) = 15.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 32 × 15.0 / (15 + 15.0) = 16.0 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 60 = 0.267 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 60 = 4.27 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (15.0 Ω) to obtain 16.0 V.

items.stem: Connecting a 840 Ω resistive load across the 280 Ω lower section of a 90 Ω–280 Ω divider in a fuel-float rheostat driving a gauge coil supplied at 23 V (ideal) pulls down the output p.d. What electrical power is delivered to the 840 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (280 × 840)/(280 + 840) = 210 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 23 × 210 / (90 + 210) = 16.1 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 840 = 0.0192 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 840 = 0.309 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (210 Ω) to obtain 0.309 W.

items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (16 × 48)/(16 + 48) = 12.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 16 × 12.0 / (8 + 12.0) = 9.60 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 48 = 0.200 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 48 = 1.92 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (12.0 Ω) to obtain 0.200 A.

items.stem: Within a joystick goniometer divider with load resistor, a 168 Ω load bridges the 56 Ω resistor of a series divider completed by a 16 Ω resistor across an ideal 29 V rail. What loaded output potential difference appears across the 168 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (56 × 168)/(56 + 168) = 42.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 29 × 42.0 / (16 + 42.0) = 21.0 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 168 = 0.125 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 168 = 2.63 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (42.0 Ω) to obtain 21.0 V.

items.stem: A pressure-transducer excitation divider uses 55 Ω and 75 Ω divider resistors across an ideal 13 V DC source, with a 150 Ω external load wired in parallel across the 75 Ω arm as shown. What electrical power is delivered to the 150 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (75 × 150)/(75 + 150) = 50.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 13 × 50.0 / (55 + 50.0) = 6.19 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 150 = 0.0413 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 150 = 0.255 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (50.0 Ω) to obtain 0.255 W.

items.stem: In the chart-recorder range-attenuator network schematic, a 100 Ω–60 Ω potential divider across 14 V (ideal) is shunted across its 60 Ω lower arm by a 120 Ω load resistor. What current flows through the 120 Ω load branch?

items.stem: An ideal 30 V cell powers a galvanometer damping-tap potential divider where upper resistor 8 Ω feeds the parallel combination of lower divider arm 60 Ω and load 120 Ω. What electrical power is delivered to the 120 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Parallel combination of lower arm and load: R_p = (60 × 120)/(60 + 120) = 40.0 Ω. Loaded output V_out = 30 × 40.0 / (8 + 40.0) = 25.0 V. Load current I_load = V_out / 120 = 0.208 A and load power P_load = V_out² / 120 = 5.21 W.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for parallel loading (40.0 Ω) to obtain 5.21 W.

items.stem: A starter-solenoid test battery of emf 26 V and internal resistance 3.4 Ω is wired directly across a 7 Ω external resistor, as shown. What is the terminal potential difference across the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 26 / (7 + 3.4) = 2.50 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 26 − (2.50)(3.4) = 17.5 V. External load power P = I² R = 43.8 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 17.5 V.

items.stem: In the schematic for a portable defibrillator battery module, a non-ideal cell (ε = 17 V, r = 2.5 Ω) supplies a single 14.5 Ω resistive load. What power is dissipated in the 14.5 Ω external load?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 17 / (14.5 + 2.5) = 1.00 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 17 − (1.00)(2.5) = 14.5 V. External load power P = I² R = 14.5 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 14.5 W.

items.stem: Load-testing an electric-scooter auxiliary battery rated at emf 17.81 V with 2.2 Ω internal resistance, a technician connects a 11.5 Ω resistor across its terminals. What is the terminal potential difference across the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 17.81 / (11.5 + 2.2) = 1.30 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 17.81 − (1.30)(2.2) = 14.9 V. External load power P = I² R = 19.4 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 14.9 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies I = ε / (R + r).
Obtains I = 3.10 A.

Obtains V = 72.8 V.

items.stem: During a variable-resistor cell characterisation practical (modelled by source V with internal and load resistances R in series), terminal p.d. is 23.4 V at current 1.2 A and drops to 10.2 V when current increases to 5.6 A. What is the internal resistance of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (23.4 − 10.2)/(5.6 − 1.2) = 3.00 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 23.4 + (1.2)(3.00) = 27.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 3.00 Ω.

items.stem: In an MPPT solar-module bench test, ideal meters across a constant-r source record V_1 = 17 V when I_1 = 1.2 A, and V_2 = 6.6 V when I_2 = 4.4 A. What is the electromotive force (emf) of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (17 − 6.6)/(4.4 − 1.2) = 3.25 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 17 + (1.2)(3.25) = 20.9 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 20.9 V.

items.stem: Switching between two load settings in a fuel-cell polarisation-curve check (series loop shown) changes the current from 1.6 A to 3.2 A while terminal voltage falls from 14.2 V to 12.6 V. What is the internal resistance of the source?

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 1.00 Ω.

items.stem: During an electrochemical cell coursework investigation (modelled by source V with internal and load resistances R in series), terminal p.d. is 10.6 V at current 1 A and drops to 7.8 V when current increases to 2.6 A. What is the electromotive force (emf) of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (10.6 − 7.8)/(2.6 − 1) = 1.75 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 10.6 + (1)(1.75) = 12.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 12.3 V.

items.stem: A battery of emf 72 V and internal resistance 3 Ω powers an off-grid cabin DC lighting and pump bus made of a 9 Ω series resistor and parallel 20 Ω and 30 Ω branches, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 50 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (20 × 30)/(20 + 30) = 12.0 Ω, R_ext = 9 + 12.0 = 21.0 Ω, and R_tot = 21.0 + 3 = 24.0 Ω. Current I = 72 / 24.0 = 3.00 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 72 − (3.00)(3) = 63.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 9.45 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 9.45 × 10³ J.

items.stem: In the lunar rover heater and transceiver bus diagram, a non-ideal source (ε = 45 V, r = 3 Ω) feeds a 6 Ω line resistor ahead of parallel 36 Ω and 12 Ω loads. What is the battery's terminal potential difference during steady 90 s operation?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (36 × 12)/(36 + 12) = 9.00 Ω, R_ext = 6 + 9.00 = 15.0 Ω, and R_tot = 15.0 + 3 = 18.0 Ω. Current I = 45 / 18.0 = 2.50 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 45 − (2.50)(3) = 37.5 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 8.44 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 37.5 V.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a glacier-monitoring battery power stage: emf 19.2 V with internal resistance 1 Ω energises a 3 Ω series element and parallel 21 Ω and 28 Ω arms. What is the battery's terminal potential difference during steady 30 s operation?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (21 × 28)/(21 + 28) = 12.0 Ω, R_ext = 3 + 12.0 = 15.0 Ω, and R_tot = 15.0 + 1 = 16.0 Ω. Current I = 19.2 / 16.0 = 1.20 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 19.2 − (1.20)(1) = 18.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 648 J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 18.0 V.

items.stem: An arctic lidar heater-and-blower battery bus connects parallel 9 Ω and 18 Ω loads via a 2 Ω series resistor to a 15 V cell of internal resistance 2 Ω. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 30 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (9 × 18)/(9 + 18) = 6.00 Ω, R_ext = 2 + 6.00 = 8.00 Ω, and R_tot = 8.00 + 2 = 10.0 Ω. Current I = 15 / 10.0 = 1.50 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 15 − (1.50)(2) = 12.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 540 J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 540 J.

items.stem: A battery of emf 117 V and internal resistance 3 Ω powers a mobile blood-bank compressor DC loop made of a 6 Ω series resistor and parallel 45 Ω and 90 Ω branches, as shown. What is the battery's terminal potential difference during steady 50 s operation?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (45 × 90)/(45 + 90) = 30.0 Ω, R_ext = 6 + 30.0 = 36.0 Ω, and R_tot = 36.0 + 3 = 39.0 Ω. Current I = 117 / 39.0 = 3.00 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 117 − (3.00)(3) = 108 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 1.62 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 108 V.

items.stem: Over a 90 s cycle of a railway track-side battery cabinet, a 34 V battery (2 Ω internal resistance) drives a 7 Ω resistor in series with parallel 12 Ω and 24 Ω resistors. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 90 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (12 × 24)/(12 + 24) = 8.00 Ω, R_ext = 7 + 8.00 = 15.0 Ω, and R_tot = 15.0 + 2 = 17.0 Ω. Current I = 34 / 17.0 = 2.00 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 34 − (2.00)(2) = 30.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 5.40 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 5.40 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_ext = 17.0 Ω and adds 2 Ω internal resistance.

Uses E_ext = V_term I × 20.
Obtains E_ext = 340 J.

items.stem: In a foam-cutting hot-wire bench rig, a uniform cylindrical nichrome wire R_1 of resistivity 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m, length 3.6 m, and diameter 0.34 mm is wired directly across an ideal 24 V DC source, as shown. What is the electrical resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = π(0.34 × 10⁻³ / 2)² = 9.08 × 10⁻⁸ m². Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 43.6 Ω. Current I = 24 / 43.6 = 0.550 A, and power P = V² / R_1 = 13.2 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 43.6 Ω.

items.stem: Element R_1 in the micrometer wire-resistivity practical schematic is a cylindrical constantan wire (resistivity 4.90 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) of length 1.5 m and circular diameter 0.52 mm connected to an ideal 18 V cell. What steady current passes through R_1?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = π(0.52 × 10⁻³ / 2)² = 2.12 × 10⁻⁷ m². Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 3.46 Ω. Current I = 18 / 3.46 = 5.20 A, and power P = V² / R_1 = 93.6 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 5.20 A.

items.stem: A 4.65 m cylindrical manganin wire of diameter 0.76 mm and resistivity 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m acts as load R_1 inside a camera-lens anti-fog heater ring energised at 12 V (ideal). What thermal power is dissipated in R_1?

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 29.3 W.

items.stem: Refer to the diagram of a precision current-shunt calibration loop: R_1 is a uniform cupronickel wire of circular cross-section (diameter 0.64 mm, length 2.2 m, resistivity 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) across 3 V (ideal). What thermal power is dissipated in R_1?

items.stem: In a spectrometer slit-warmer wire element, a uniform cylindrical titanium wire R_1 of resistivity 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, length 4.3 m, and diameter 0.7 mm is wired directly across an ideal 15 V DC source, as shown. What is the electrical resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = π(0.7 × 10⁻³ / 2)² = 3.85 × 10⁻⁷ m². Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 4.69 Ω. Current I = 15 / 4.69 = 3.20 A, and power P = V² / R_1 = 47.9 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 4.69 Ω.

items.stem: Element R_1 in the micro-thruster catalyst bed heater schematic is a cylindrical cupronickel wire (resistivity 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) of length 3.25 m and circular diameter 0.64 mm connected to an ideal 9 V cell. What steady current passes through R_1?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = π(0.64 × 10⁻³ / 2)² = 3.22 × 10⁻⁷ m². Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 3.84 Ω. Current I = 9 / 3.84 = 2.34 A, and power P = V² / R_1 = 21.1 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = π d² / 4 and R = ρL / A to obtain 2.34 A.

items.stem: A slide-wire potentiometer rail places a 5 Ω reference resistor in series with a uniform stainless-steel wire R_1 (resistivity 7.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, length 4.4 m, area 3.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) across an ideal 17 V DC source, as shown. What is the potential difference across the stainless-steel wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = (7.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m)(4.4) / (3.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 10.6 Ω. Series current I = 17 / (5 + 10.6) = 1.09 A, and p.d. across the wire V_1 = I R_1 = 11.5 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes R_1 = 10.6 Ω and obtains 11.5 V.

items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = (1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m)(4) / (5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 8.00 Ω. Series current I = 22 / (14 + 8.00) = 1.00 A, and p.d. across the wire V_1 = I R_1 = 8.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes R_1 = 8.00 Ω and obtains 1.00 A.

items.stem: An ideal 15 V cell drives a micro-balance restoring-coil feed made of a 7 Ω resistor in series with platinum-iridium wire R_1 (length 4.8 m, area 4.50 × 10⁻⁷ m², resistivity 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m). What is the potential difference across the platinum-iridium wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = (2.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m)(4.8) / (4.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) = 2.67 Ω. Series current I = 15 / (7 + 2.67) = 1.55 A, and p.d. across the wire V_1 = I R_1 = 4.14 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes R_1 = 2.67 Ω and obtains 4.14 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes R_1 = 2.93 Ω and obtains 7.97 V.

items.stem: In a shunted ammeter manganin bypass assembly, a uniform cupronickel wire R_1 (resistivity 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, length 2.5 m, area 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m²) lies in parallel with a 8 Ω shunt, fed via a 4 Ω series resistor from an ideal 10 V DC source. What current passes through the cupronickel wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 1.90 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 8)/(R_1 + 8) = 1.54 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 4 + 1.54 = 5.54 Ω; main current I_tot = 1.81 A, V_p = 2.77 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 1.46 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 1.90 Ω and obtains 1.46 A.

items.stem: Within a galvanometer shunt calibration cell, current from an ideal 24 V cell traverses a 4 Ω resistor before splitting between nichrome wire R_1 (2 m, 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ m², 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m) and a 6 Ω shunt. What is the combined resistance of R_1 and the 6 Ω shunt in parallel?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 8.80 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 6)/(R_1 + 6) = 3.57 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 4 + 3.57 = 7.57 Ω; main current I_tot = 3.17 A, V_p = 11.3 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 1.29 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 8.80 Ω and obtains 3.57 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 5.72 Ω and obtains 1.48 A.

items.stem: In a vacuum-evaporator shunted filament holder, a uniform manganin wire R_1 (resistivity 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, length 2.5 m, area 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) lies in parallel with a 5 Ω shunt, fed via a 2 Ω series resistor from an ideal 29 V DC source. What is the combined resistance of R_1 and the 5 Ω shunt in parallel?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 1.85 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 5)/(R_1 + 5) = 1.35 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 2 + 1.35 = 3.35 Ω; main current I_tot = 8.66 A, V_p = 11.7 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 6.33 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 1.85 Ω and obtains 1.35 Ω.

items.stem: A 2 m kanthal wire R_1 of area 3.50 × 10⁻⁷ m² and resistivity 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m is shunted by a 7 Ω resistor in a battery-cycler current-sense shunt network behind a 6 Ω series ballast across 21 V (ideal). What is the combined resistance of R_1 and the 7 Ω shunt in parallel?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 8.29 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 7)/(R_1 + 7) = 3.79 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 6 + 3.79 = 9.79 Ω; main current I_tot = 2.14 A, V_p = 8.14 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 0.982 A.

items.stem: Within a welding-cable current-diverter rig, current from an ideal 10 V cell traverses a 5 Ω resistor before splitting between cupronickel wire R_1 (5.5 m, 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) and a 23 Ω shunt. What current passes through the cupronickel wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 3.48 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 23)/(R_1 + 23) = 3.03 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 5 + 3.03 = 8.03 Ω; main current I_tot = 1.25 A, V_p = 3.77 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 1.08 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 3.48 Ω and obtains 1.08 A.

items.stem: Refer to a magnet-power-supply trim-shunt stage shown: parallel arms R_1 (titanium, length 6.5 m, area 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², ρ = 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) and 15 Ω connect through 8 Ω to an ideal 21 V rail. What is the combined resistance of R_1 and the 15 Ω shunt in parallel?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 5.46 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 15)/(R_1 + 15) = 4.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 8 + 4.00 = 12.0 Ω; main current I_tot = 1.75 A, V_p = 7.00 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 1.28 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 5.46 Ω and obtains 4.00 Ω.

items.stem: In an electrolysis-cell bypass resistor bank, a uniform platinum-iridium wire R_1 (resistivity 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, length 2 m, area 5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m²) lies in parallel with a 4 Ω shunt, fed via a 10 Ω series resistor from an ideal 28 V DC source. What current passes through the platinum-iridium wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 0.909 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 4)/(R_1 + 4) = 0.741 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 10 + 0.741 = 10.7 Ω; main current I_tot = 2.61 A, V_p = 1.93 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 2.12 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 0.909 Ω and obtains 2.12 A.

items.stem: A 3 m constantan wire R_1 of area 3.50 × 10⁻⁷ m² and resistivity 4.90 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m is shunted by a 15 Ω resistor in a mass-flow thermal bypass sensor behind a 5 Ω series ballast across 10 V (ideal). What current passes through the constantan wire R_1?
items.workedSolution: Wire resistance R_1 = ρL / A = 4.20 Ω. Parallel resistance R_p = (R_1 × 15)/(R_1 + 15) = 3.28 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 5 + 3.28 = 8.28 Ω; main current I_tot = 1.21 A, V_p = 3.96 V, and wire current I_1 = V_p / R_1 = 0.943 A.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 4.20 Ω and obtains 0.943 A.

items.stem: In the schematic for a laser-flashlamp simmer-shunt network, an ideal 29 V source feeds a 10 Ω series resistor followed by parallel branches consisting of titanium wire R_1 (L = 2 m, A = 3.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², ρ = 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) and a 23 Ω resistor.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_1 = 2.80 Ω and combines in parallel with 23 Ω.
Obtains R_p = 2.50 Ω.

Obtains I_tot = 2.32 A.
Finds V_p and uses P_1 = V_p² / R_1.
Obtains P_1 = 12.0 W.

items.stem: An immersive calorimetry heating coil uses a battery of emf 38.6 V and internal resistance 1.3 Ω wired across a 18 Ω heating load, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the 18 Ω load during 60 s?

items.stem: In a de-icing heater manifold on a weather mast, an ideal 6.4 V DC source drives a 5 Ω limiting resistor connected in series with parallel 4 Ω and 12 Ω resistors, as shown. What electrical power is dissipated in the 12 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 5 + 3.00 = 8.00 Ω. Supply current I = 6.4 / 8.00 = 0.800 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 0.800 × 3.00 = 2.40 V. Power in 12 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 12 = 0.480 W.

items.stem: While bench-testing a dual-zone incubator heating stage, an engineer wires a 3 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 12 Ω and 36 Ω resistors across an ideal 6 V supply. What potential difference develops across the parallel 12 Ω and 36 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (12 × 36)/(12 + 36) = 9.00 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 6 × 9.00 / (3 + 9.00) = 4.50 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 9.00 Ω and finds V_p = 4.50 V.

items.stem: An ideal 39 V power unit energises a submersible ROV auxiliary power bus made from a 7 Ω series element followed by 8 Ω and 24 Ω resistors in parallel, as illustrated. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (8 × 24)/(8 + 24) = 6.00 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 7 + 6.00 = 13.0 Ω. Supply current I = 39 / 13.0 = 3.00 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 7 Ω with R_p = 6.00 Ω to obtain I = 3.00 A.

items.stem: Parallel resistors of 28 Ω and 84 Ω inside a precision optical-table thermal stabiliser receive current through a 2 Ω series resistor from an ideal 46 V cell. What electrical power is dissipated in the 84 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (28 × 84)/(28 + 84) = 21.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 2 + 21.0 = 23.0 Ω. Supply current I = 46 / 23.0 = 2.00 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 2.00 × 21.0 = 42.0 V. Power in 84 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 84 = 21.0 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 42.0 V and calculates P = 21.0 W.

items.stem: A greenhouse misting-valve controller operates from an ideal 27.6 V rail; current traverses a 13 Ω ballast resistor before splitting across 14 Ω and 35 Ω parallel arms. What potential difference develops across the parallel 14 Ω and 35 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (14 × 35)/(14 + 35) = 10.0 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 27.6 × 10.0 / (13 + 10.0) = 12.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 10.0 Ω and finds V_p = 12.0 V.

items.stem: Examine the circuit for a vacuum-chamber bakeout resistor assembly, where a 7 Ω resistor stands in series with parallel 4 Ω and 12 Ω branches across an ideal 8 V source. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3.00 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 7 + 3.00 = 10.0 Ω. Supply current I = 8 / 10.0 = 0.800 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 7 Ω with R_p = 3.00 Ω to obtain I = 0.800 A.

items.stem: In a traction-motor dynamic braking test bank, an ideal 57 V DC source drives a 13 Ω limiting resistor connected in series with parallel 18 Ω and 9 Ω resistors, as shown. What electrical power is dissipated in the 9 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (18 × 9)/(18 + 9) = 6.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 13 + 6.00 = 19.0 Ω. Supply current I = 57 / 19.0 = 3.00 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 3.00 × 6.00 = 18.0 V. Power in 9 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 9 = 36.0 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 18.0 V and calculates P = 36.0 W.

items.stem: While bench-testing a balloon telemetry heater loop, an engineer wires a 18 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 14 Ω and 35 Ω resistors across an ideal 33.6 V supply. What potential difference develops across the parallel 14 Ω and 35 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (14 × 35)/(14 + 35) = 10.0 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 33.6 × 10.0 / (18 + 10.0) = 12.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 10.0 Ω and finds V_p = 12.0 V.

items.stem: An ideal 48 V power unit energises an industrial kiln damper actuator network made from a 14 Ω series element followed by 24 Ω and 48 Ω resistors in parallel, as illustrated. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (24 × 48)/(24 + 48) = 16.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 14 + 16.0 = 30.0 Ω. Supply current I = 48 / 30.0 = 1.60 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 14 Ω with R_p = 16.0 Ω to obtain I = 1.60 A.

items.stem: Parallel resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω inside a cryogenic transfer-line warm-up harness receive current through a 15 Ω series resistor from an ideal 43.2 V cell. What electrical power is dissipated in the 12 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 15 + 3.00 = 18.0 Ω. Supply current I = 43.2 / 18.0 = 2.40 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 2.40 × 3.00 = 7.20 V. Power in 12 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 12 = 4.32 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 7.20 V and calculates P = 4.32 W.

items.stem: An automatic street-lamp twilight switch uses an ideal 5 V DC supply, an LDR, and a 6 kΩ fixed resistor wired as shown, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. The LDR resistance is 64 kΩ in darkness and 1.5 kΩ in bright light. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 64 + 6 = 70 kΩ, so I_dark = 5 / 70000 = 7.14 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.429 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 5 × 6 / (1.5 + 6) = 4.00 V.

items.stem: In the greenhouse shade-curtain controller diagram, an LDR (90 kΩ dark; 3.5 kΩ bright) sits in series with a 4 kΩ resistor across an ideal 18 V cell while ideal voltmeter Vout monitors the 4 kΩ resistor. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 90 + 4 = 94 kΩ, so I_dark = 18 / 94000 = 1.91 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.766 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 18 × 4 / (3.5 + 4) = 9.60 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 4 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.766 V.

items.stem: Testing a museum light-exposure alarm circuit supplied at 6 V (ideal), illumination lowers the LDR resistance from 123 kΩ in darkness to 2.5 kΩ in bright light; Vout is measured across the series 4 kΩ resistor. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 123 + 4 = 127 kΩ, so I_dark = 6 / 127000 = 4.72 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.189 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 6 × 4 / (2.5 + 4) = 3.69 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 4 kΩ resistor to obtain 4.72 × 10⁻⁵ A.

items.stem: The sensing stage of a photographic darkroom door interlock connects an LDR (69 kΩ in darkness, 0.8 kΩ when brightly lit) and a 2 kΩ resistor across an ideal 6 V source, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 69 + 2 = 71 kΩ, so I_dark = 6 / 71000 = 8.45 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.169 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 6 × 2 / (0.8 + 2) = 4.29 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 2 kΩ resistor to obtain 4.29 V.

items.stem: An ideal 9 V rail powers a solar tracker dusk-detection stage comprising an LDR (81 kΩ dark, 0.5 kΩ bright) in series with a 8 kΩ output resistor bridged by ideal voltmeter Vout. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 81 + 8 = 89 kΩ, so I_dark = 9 / 89000 = 1.01 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.809 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 9 × 8 / (0.5 + 8) = 8.47 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 8 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.809 V.

items.stem: Within a poultry-house lighting relay, an ideal voltmeter Vout spans a 2 kΩ resistor in series with an LDR (36 kΩ in darkness; 0.8 kΩ in bright daylight) across an ideal 24 V supply. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 36 + 2 = 38 kΩ, so I_dark = 24 / 38000 = 6.32 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 1.26 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 24 × 2 / (0.8 + 2) = 17.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 2 kΩ resistor to obtain 6.32 × 10⁻⁴ A.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a warehouse skylight dimming sensor: an LDR whose resistance changes between 39 kΩ (dark) and 1.2 kΩ (bright) forms a divider with a 6 kΩ resistor across 5 V (ideal). What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 39 + 6 = 45 kΩ, so I_dark = 5 / 45000 = 1.11 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.667 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 5 × 6 / (1.2 + 6) = 4.17 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 6 kΩ resistor to obtain 4.17 V.

items.stem: A conveyor-belt optical package counter uses an ideal 12 V DC supply, an LDR, and a 12 kΩ fixed resistor wired as shown, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. The LDR resistance is 87 kΩ in darkness and 1.5 kΩ in bright light. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 87 + 12 = 99 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 99000 = 1.21 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 1.45 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 12 / (1.5 + 12) = 10.7 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 12 kΩ resistor to obtain 1.45 V.

items.stem: Testing a meteorological sunshine-duration logger supplied at 9 V (ideal), illumination lowers the LDR resistance from 160 kΩ in darkness to 0.8 kΩ in bright light; Vout is measured across the series 2 kΩ resistor. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 160 + 2 = 162 kΩ, so I_dark = 9 / 162000 = 5.56 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.111 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 9 × 2 / (0.8 + 2) = 6.43 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 2 kΩ resistor to obtain 6.43 V.

items.stem: The sensing stage of a stairwell dusk-to-dawn LED trigger connects an LDR (128 kΩ in darkness, 0.8 kΩ when brightly lit) and a 20 kΩ resistor across an ideal 6 V source, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 128 + 20 = 148 kΩ, so I_dark = 6 / 148000 = 4.05 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.811 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 6 × 20 / (0.8 + 20) = 5.77 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.811 V.

items.stem: An ideal 6 V rail powers a highway tunnel entrance luminance monitor comprising an LDR (59 kΩ dark, 0.8 kΩ bright) in series with a 10 kΩ output resistor bridged by ideal voltmeter Vout. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 59 + 10 = 69 kΩ, so I_dark = 6 / 69000 = 8.70 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.870 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 6 × 10 / (0.8 + 10) = 5.56 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 10 kΩ resistor to obtain 8.70 × 10⁻⁵ A.

items.stem: Within an aquarium photoperiod timer sensor, an ideal voltmeter Vout spans a 6 kΩ resistor in series with an LDR (55 kΩ in darkness; 1 kΩ in bright daylight) across an ideal 15 V supply. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a railway level-crossing beacon dimmer: an LDR whose resistance changes between 66 kΩ (dark) and 1.2 kΩ (bright) forms a divider with a 4 kΩ resistor across 18 V (ideal). What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 66 + 4 = 70 kΩ, so I_dark = 18 / 70000 = 2.57 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 1.03 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 18 × 4 / (1.2 + 4) = 13.8 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 4 kΩ resistor to obtain 1.03 V.

items.stem: In a neonatal incubator thermal-alarm divider, an NTC thermistor (resistance decreases as temperature rises) has resistance 170 Ω at the operating point and sits in series with a 600 Ω fixed resistor across an ideal 12 V DC supply, as shown. What potential difference appears across the 170 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 600 + 170 = 770 Ω. Current I = 12 / 770 = 0.0156 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 12 × 170 / 770 = 2.65 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0413 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 2.65 V.

items.stem: An NTC thermistor R_1 (resistance decreases with rising temperature) sits in series with a 1080 Ω resistor across an ideal 16 V source in a lithium-ion pack over-temperature cutoff, as shown. When an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 4.00 V, what is the resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 1080 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 16 − 4.00 = 12.0 V. Current I = 12.0 / 1080 = 0.0111 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 4.00 / 0.0111 = 360 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 12.0 V to find I = 0.0111 A and R_1 = 360 Ω.

items.stem: The divider stage of an engine-coolant sensing bridge wires a 190 Ω reference resistor in series with an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient; 1120 Ω at the test temperature) across an ideal 5 V source. What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 1120 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 190 + 1120 = 1310 Ω. Current I = 5 / 1310 = 3.82 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 5 × 1120 / 1310 = 4.27 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0163 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.0163 W.

items.stem: In the 3D-printer hot-end thermistor loop diagram, R_1 is an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) wired in series with a 510 Ω precision resistor across an ideal 20 V supply. At an operating point where the p.d. across R_1 is 14.0 V, calculate R_1.
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 510 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 20 − 14.0 = 6.00 V. Current I = 6.00 / 510 = 0.0118 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 14.0 / 0.0118 = 1.19 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 6.00 V to find I = 0.0118 A and R_1 = 1.19 × 10³ Ω.
