items.stem: During steady-state calibration of a fermentation vat temperature regulator, an ideal 5 V cell drives a 200 Ω resistor in series with a 270 Ω NTC thermistor (whose resistance falls with increasing temperature). What potential difference appears across the 270 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 200 + 270 = 470 Ω. Current I = 5 / 470 = 0.0106 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 5 × 270 / 470 = 2.87 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0306 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 2.87 V.

items.stem: Monitoring a quartz-crystal oven controller driven by an ideal 24 V cell, a technician records 9.00 V on an ideal voltmeter across NTC thermistor R_1 (whose resistance drops when warmed) in series with 450 Ω. What is R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 450 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 24 − 9.00 = 15.0 V. Current I = 15.0 / 450 = 0.0333 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 9.00 / 0.0333 = 270 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 15.0 V to find I = 0.0333 A and R_1 = 270 Ω.

items.stem: An ideal 15 V rail powers an espresso boiler thermal-feedback divider containing a 280 Ω series resistor and an NTC thermistor (resistance 350 Ω, decreasing when heated). What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 350 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 280 + 350 = 630 Ω. Current I = 15 / 630 = 0.0238 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 15 × 350 / 630 = 8.33 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.198 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.198 W.

items.stem: In a server-blade heatsink thermal monitor, an NTC thermistor (resistance decreases as temperature rises) has resistance 990 Ω at the operating point and sits in series with a 420 Ω fixed resistor across an ideal 9 V DC supply, as shown. What potential difference appears across the 990 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 420 + 990 = 1410 Ω. Current I = 9 / 1410 = 6.38 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 9 × 990 / 1410 = 6.32 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0403 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 6.32 V.

items.stem: An NTC thermistor R_1 (resistance decreases with rising temperature) sits in series with a 1380 Ω resistor across an ideal 18 V source in a water-bath thermostat calibration circuit, as shown. When an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 6.00 V, what is the resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 1380 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 18 − 6.00 = 12.0 V. Current I = 12.0 / 1380 = 8.70 × 10⁻³ A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 6.00 / 8.70 × 10⁻³ = 690 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 12.0 V to find I = 8.70 × 10⁻³ A and R_1 = 690 Ω.

items.stem: During steady-state calibration of a wind-turbine gearbox oil-temperature probe, an ideal 9 V cell drives a 360 Ω resistor in series with a 750 Ω NTC thermistor (whose resistance falls with increasing temperature). What potential difference appears across the 750 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 360 + 750 = 1110 Ω. Current I = 9 / 1110 = 8.11 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 9 × 750 / 1110 = 6.08 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0493 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 6.08 V.

items.stem: Monitoring a satellite battery-deck thermistor divider driven by an ideal 20 V cell, a technician records 12.0 V on an ideal voltmeter across NTC thermistor R_1 (whose resistance drops when warmed) in series with 960 Ω. What is R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 960 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 20 − 12.0 = 8.00 V. Current I = 8.00 / 960 = 8.33 × 10⁻³ A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 12.0 / 8.33 × 10⁻³ = 1.44 × 10³ Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 8.00 V to find I = 8.33 × 10⁻³ A and R_1 = 1.44 × 10³ Ω.

items.stem: An ideal 12 V rail powers a blood-warmer safety cutoff divider containing a 590 Ω series resistor and an NTC thermistor (resistance 710 Ω, decreasing when heated). What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 710 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 590 + 710 = 1300 Ω. Current I = 12 / 1300 = 9.23 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 12 × 710 / 1300 = 6.55 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0605 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.0605 W.

items.stem: A starter-solenoid test battery of emf 8.93 V and internal resistance 0.7 Ω is wired directly across a 4 Ω external resistor, as shown. What is the terminal potential difference across the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 8.93 / (4 + 0.7) = 1.90 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 8.93 − (1.90)(0.7) = 7.60 V. External load power P = I² R = 14.4 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 7.60 V.

items.stem: In the schematic for a portable defibrillator battery module, a non-ideal cell (ε = 47.12 V, r = 1.3 Ω) supplies a single 23.5 Ω resistive load. What power is dissipated in the 23.5 Ω external load?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 47.12 / (23.5 + 1.3) = 1.90 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 47.12 − (1.90)(1.3) = 44.6 V. External load power P = I² R = 84.8 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 84.8 W.

items.stem: Load-testing a field transceiver LiFePO4 pack rated at emf 30.02 V with 2.8 Ω internal resistance, a technician connects a 13 Ω resistor across its terminals. What current is delivered by the battery?

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 1.90 A.

items.stem: The circuit models a cordless drill high-drain battery as an ideal 16.25 V source in series with 1 Ω internal resistance driving a 5.5 Ω load. What is the terminal potential difference across the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 16.25 / (5.5 + 1) = 2.50 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 16.25 − (2.50)(1) = 13.8 V. External load power P = I² R = 34.4 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 13.8 V.

items.stem: The circuit models a weather-buoy primary lithium cell as an ideal 18.26 V source in series with 1.3 Ω internal resistance driving a 7 Ω load. What power is dissipated in the 7 Ω external load?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 18.26 / (7 + 1.3) = 2.20 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 18.26 − (2.20)(1.3) = 15.4 V. External load power P = I² R = 33.9 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 33.9 W.

items.stem: During a variable-resistor cell characterisation practical (modelled by source V with internal and load resistances R in series), terminal p.d. is 21 V at current 1.4 A and drops to 13.8 V when current increases to 4.6 A. What is the internal resistance of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (21 − 13.8)/(4.6 − 1.4) = 2.25 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 21 + (1.4)(2.25) = 24.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 2.25 Ω.

items.stem: In an MPPT solar-module bench test, ideal meters across a constant-r source record V_1 = 19.6 V when I_1 = 1.2 A, and V_2 = 12.6 V when I_2 = 4 A. What is the electromotive force (emf) of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (19.6 − 12.6)/(4 − 1.2) = 2.50 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 19.6 + (1.2)(2.50) = 22.6 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 22.6 V.

items.stem: In a Daniel-cell internal-resistance lab, ideal meters across a constant-r source record V_1 = 6.7 V when I_1 = 0.6 A, and V_2 = 4.2 V when I_2 = 2.6 A. What is the internal resistance of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (6.7 − 4.2)/(2.6 − 0.6) = 1.25 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 6.7 + (0.6)(1.25) = 7.45 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 1.25 Ω.

items.stem: A battery of emf 13.6 V and internal resistance 3 Ω powers an off-grid cabin DC lighting and pump bus made of a 4 Ω series resistor and parallel 15 Ω and 30 Ω branches, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 90 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (15 × 30)/(15 + 30) = 10.0 Ω, R_ext = 4 + 10.0 = 14.0 Ω, and R_tot = 14.0 + 3 = 17.0 Ω. Current I = 13.6 / 17.0 = 0.800 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 13.6 − (0.800)(3) = 11.2 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 806 J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 806 J.

items.stem: In the lunar rover heater and transceiver bus diagram, a non-ideal source (ε = 20 V, r = 3 Ω) feeds a 2 Ω line resistor ahead of parallel 20 Ω and 60 Ω loads. What is the battery's terminal potential difference during steady 60 s operation?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (20 × 60)/(20 + 60) = 15.0 Ω, R_ext = 2 + 15.0 = 17.0 Ω, and R_tot = 17.0 + 3 = 20.0 Ω. Current I = 20 / 20.0 = 1.00 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 20 − (1.00)(3) = 17.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 1.02 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 17.0 V.

items.stem: A field-hospital DC distribution unit connects parallel 45 Ω and 90 Ω loads via a 3 Ω series resistor to a 42 V cell of internal resistance 2 Ω. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 30 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (45 × 90)/(45 + 90) = 30.0 Ω, R_ext = 3 + 30.0 = 33.0 Ω, and R_tot = 33.0 + 2 = 35.0 Ω. Current I = 42 / 35.0 = 1.20 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 42 − (1.20)(2) = 39.6 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 1.43 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 1.43 × 10³ J.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a glacier-monitoring battery power stage: emf 51 V with internal resistance 3.5 Ω energises a 10 Ω series element and parallel 15 Ω and 60 Ω arms. What is the battery's terminal potential difference during steady 90 s operation?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (15 × 60)/(15 + 60) = 12.0 Ω, R_ext = 10 + 12.0 = 22.0 Ω, and R_tot = 22.0 + 3.5 = 25.5 Ω. Current I = 51 / 25.5 = 2.00 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 51 − (2.00)(3.5) = 44.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 7.92 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 44.0 V.

items.stem: In the forestry fire-tower radio and beacon bus diagram, a non-ideal source (ε = 30 V, r = 2 Ω) feeds a 4 Ω line resistor ahead of parallel 9 Ω and 18 Ω loads. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 15 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (9 × 18)/(9 + 18) = 6.00 Ω, R_ext = 4 + 6.00 = 10.0 Ω, and R_tot = 10.0 + 2 = 12.0 Ω. Current I = 30 / 12.0 = 2.50 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 30 − (2.50)(2) = 25.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 938 J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 938 J.

items.stem: Over a 15 s cycle of a railway track-side battery cabinet, a 51 V battery (3 Ω internal resistance) drives a 8 Ω resistor in series with parallel 10 Ω and 15 Ω resistors. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 15 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (10 × 15)/(10 + 15) = 6.00 Ω, R_ext = 8 + 6.00 = 14.0 Ω, and R_tot = 14.0 + 3 = 17.0 Ω. Current I = 51 / 17.0 = 3.00 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 51 − (3.00)(3) = 42.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 1.89 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 1.89 × 10³ J.

items.stem: A cave-rescue repeater battery network connects parallel 40 Ω and 60 Ω loads via a 10 Ω series resistor to a 108 V cell of internal resistance 2 Ω. What is the battery's terminal potential difference during steady 30 s operation?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (40 × 60)/(40 + 60) = 24.0 Ω, R_ext = 10 + 24.0 = 34.0 Ω, and R_tot = 34.0 + 2 = 36.0 Ω. Current I = 108 / 36.0 = 3.00 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 108 − (3.00)(2) = 102 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 9.18 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 102 V.

items.stem: An immersive calorimetry heating coil uses a battery of emf 51.8 V and internal resistance 1.3 Ω wired across a 13.5 Ω heating load, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the 13.5 Ω load during 90 s?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 51.8 / (13.5 + 1.3) = 3.50 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 47.3 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 1.49 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 3.50 A and E_ext = I² R t = 1.49 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: Refer to a ski-boot insole heater pack illustrated: emf 36.68 V in series with internal resistance 1.3 Ω powers a 15 Ω load over 180 s. How much energy reaches the 15 Ω load?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 36.68 / (15 + 1.3) = 2.25 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 33.8 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 1.37 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 2.25 A and E_ext = I² R t = 1.37 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: A portable nebuliser heater element uses a battery of emf 27.5 V and internal resistance 1 Ω wired across a 21 Ω heating load, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the 21 Ω load during 150 s?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 27.5 / (21 + 1) = 1.25 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 26.3 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 4.92 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 1.25 A and E_ext = I² R t = 4.92 × 10³ J.

items.stem: In the laboratory oil-bath immersion coil diagram, a cell (ε = 45.65 V, r = 1.6 Ω) supplies a 15 Ω external resistor steadily for 45 s. What total energy is delivered to the 15 Ω resistor?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 45.65 / (15 + 1.6) = 2.75 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 41.3 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 5.10 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 2.75 A and E_ext = I² R t = 5.10 × 10³ J.

items.stem: In a de-icing heater manifold on a weather mast, an ideal 16.8 V DC source drives a 2 Ω limiting resistor connected in series with parallel 18 Ω and 36 Ω resistors, as shown. What electrical power is dissipated in the 36 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (18 × 36)/(18 + 36) = 12.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 2 + 12.0 = 14.0 Ω. Supply current I = 16.8 / 14.0 = 1.20 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 1.20 × 12.0 = 14.4 V. Power in 36 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 36 = 5.76 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 14.4 V and calculates P = 5.76 W.

items.stem: While bench-testing a dual-zone incubator heating stage, an engineer wires a 10 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 18 Ω and 36 Ω resistors across an ideal 26.4 V supply. What potential difference develops across the parallel 18 Ω and 36 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (18 × 36)/(18 + 36) = 12.0 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 26.4 × 12.0 / (10 + 12.0) = 14.4 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 12.0 Ω and finds V_p = 14.4 V.

items.stem: An ideal 54 V power unit energises a submersible ROV auxiliary power bus made from a 15 Ω series element followed by 28 Ω and 84 Ω resistors in parallel, as illustrated. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (28 × 84)/(28 + 84) = 21.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 15 + 21.0 = 36.0 Ω. Supply current I = 54 / 36.0 = 1.50 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 15 Ω with R_p = 21.0 Ω to obtain I = 1.50 A.

items.stem: Parallel resistors of 16 Ω and 48 Ω inside a precision optical-table thermal stabiliser receive current through a 4 Ω series resistor from an ideal 25.6 V cell. What electrical power is dissipated in the 48 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (16 × 48)/(16 + 48) = 12.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 4 + 12.0 = 16.0 Ω. Supply current I = 25.6 / 16.0 = 1.60 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 1.60 × 12.0 = 19.2 V. Power in 48 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 48 = 7.68 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 19.2 V and calculates P = 7.68 W.

items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (21 × 28)/(21 + 28) = 12.0 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 20 × 12.0 / (13 + 12.0) = 9.60 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 12.0 Ω and finds V_p = 9.60 V.

items.stem: Examine the circuit for a vacuum-chamber bakeout resistor assembly, where a 15 Ω resistor stands in series with parallel 30 Ω and 60 Ω branches across an ideal 56 V source. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (30 × 60)/(30 + 60) = 20.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 15 + 20.0 = 35.0 Ω. Supply current I = 56 / 35.0 = 1.60 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 15 Ω with R_p = 20.0 Ω to obtain I = 1.60 A.

items.stem: In a traction-motor dynamic braking test bank, an ideal 52.8 V DC source drives a 10 Ω limiting resistor connected in series with parallel 16 Ω and 48 Ω resistors, as shown. What electrical power is dissipated in the 48 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (16 × 48)/(16 + 48) = 12.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 10 + 12.0 = 22.0 Ω. Supply current I = 52.8 / 22.0 = 2.40 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 2.40 × 12.0 = 28.8 V. Power in 48 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 48 = 17.3 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 28.8 V and calculates P = 17.3 W.

items.stem: While bench-testing a balloon telemetry heater loop, an engineer wires a 16 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 4 Ω and 12 Ω resistors across an ideal 22.8 V supply. What potential difference develops across the parallel 4 Ω and 12 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3.00 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 22.8 × 3.00 / (16 + 3.00) = 3.60 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 3.00 Ω and finds V_p = 3.60 V.

items.stem: An ideal 52.5 V power unit energises an industrial kiln damper actuator network made from a 14 Ω series element followed by 28 Ω and 84 Ω resistors in parallel, as illustrated. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (28 × 84)/(28 + 84) = 21.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 14 + 21.0 = 35.0 Ω. Supply current I = 52.5 / 35.0 = 1.50 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 14 Ω with R_p = 21.0 Ω to obtain I = 1.50 A.

items.stem: Parallel resistors of 9 Ω and 18 Ω inside a cryogenic transfer-line warm-up harness receive current through a 4 Ω series resistor from an ideal 24 V cell. What electrical power is dissipated in the 18 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (9 × 18)/(9 + 18) = 6.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 4 + 6.00 = 10.0 Ω. Supply current I = 24 / 10.0 = 2.40 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 2.40 × 6.00 = 14.4 V. Power in 18 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 18 = 11.5 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 14.4 V and calculates P = 11.5 W.

items.stem: An automatic street-lamp twilight switch uses an ideal 9 V DC supply, an LDR, and a 10 kΩ fixed resistor wired as shown, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. The LDR resistance is 117 kΩ in darkness and 1.5 kΩ in bright light. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 117 + 10 = 127 kΩ, so I_dark = 9 / 127000 = 7.09 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.709 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 9 × 10 / (1.5 + 10) = 7.83 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 10 kΩ resistor to obtain 7.83 V.

items.stem: In the greenhouse shade-curtain controller diagram, an LDR (53 kΩ dark; 3.5 kΩ bright) sits in series with a 3 kΩ resistor across an ideal 9 V cell while ideal voltmeter Vout monitors the 3 kΩ resistor. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 53 + 3 = 56 kΩ, so I_dark = 9 / 56000 = 1.61 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.482 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 9 × 3 / (3.5 + 3) = 4.15 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 3 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.482 V.

items.stem: Testing a museum light-exposure alarm circuit supplied at 18 V (ideal), illumination lowers the LDR resistance from 157 kΩ in darkness to 2.5 kΩ in bright light; Vout is measured across the series 12 kΩ resistor. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 157 + 12 = 169 kΩ, so I_dark = 18 / 169000 = 1.07 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 1.28 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 18 × 12 / (2.5 + 12) = 14.9 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 12 kΩ resistor to obtain 1.07 × 10⁻⁴ A.

items.stem: The sensing stage of a photographic darkroom door interlock connects an LDR (61 kΩ in darkness, 0.8 kΩ when brightly lit) and a 8 kΩ resistor across an ideal 12 V source, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 61 + 8 = 69 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 69000 = 1.74 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 1.39 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 8 / (0.8 + 8) = 10.9 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 8 kΩ resistor to obtain 10.9 V.

items.stem: An ideal 12 V rail powers a solar tracker dusk-detection stage comprising an LDR (84 kΩ dark, 3.5 kΩ bright) in series with a 4 kΩ output resistor bridged by ideal voltmeter Vout. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 84 + 4 = 88 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 88000 = 1.36 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.545 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 4 / (3.5 + 4) = 6.40 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 4 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.545 V.

items.stem: Within a poultry-house lighting relay, an ideal voltmeter Vout spans a 20 kΩ resistor in series with an LDR (120 kΩ in darkness; 1 kΩ in bright daylight) across an ideal 12 V supply. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 120 + 20 = 140 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 140000 = 8.57 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 1.71 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 20 / (1 + 20) = 11.4 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 8.57 × 10⁻⁵ A.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a warehouse skylight dimming sensor: an LDR whose resistance changes between 109 kΩ (dark) and 1.5 kΩ (bright) forms a divider with a 15 kΩ resistor across 24 V (ideal). What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 109 + 15 = 124 kΩ, so I_dark = 24 / 124000 = 1.94 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 2.90 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 24 × 15 / (1.5 + 15) = 21.8 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 15 kΩ resistor to obtain 21.8 V.

items.stem: A conveyor-belt optical package counter uses an ideal 6 V DC supply, an LDR, and a 8 kΩ fixed resistor wired as shown, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. The LDR resistance is 44 kΩ in darkness and 2.5 kΩ in bright light. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 44 + 8 = 52 kΩ, so I_dark = 6 / 52000 = 1.15 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.923 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 6 × 8 / (2.5 + 8) = 4.57 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 8 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.923 V.

items.stem: In the observatory dome-shutter safety sensor diagram, an LDR (137 kΩ dark; 0.5 kΩ bright) sits in series with a 6 kΩ resistor across an ideal 12 V cell while ideal voltmeter Vout monitors the 6 kΩ resistor. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?

items.stem: An ideal 15 V rail powers a highway tunnel entrance luminance monitor comprising an LDR (48 kΩ dark, 1 kΩ bright) in series with a 20 kΩ output resistor bridged by ideal voltmeter Vout. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 48 + 20 = 68 kΩ, so I_dark = 15 / 68000 = 2.21 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 4.41 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 15 × 20 / (1 + 20) = 14.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 2.21 × 10⁻⁴ A.

items.stem: Within an aquarium photoperiod timer sensor, an ideal voltmeter Vout spans a 2 kΩ resistor in series with an LDR (68 kΩ in darkness; 1 kΩ in bright daylight) across an ideal 24 V supply. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 68 + 2 = 70 kΩ, so I_dark = 24 / 70000 = 3.43 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.686 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 24 × 2 / (1 + 2) = 16.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 2 kΩ resistor to obtain 16.0 V.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a railway level-crossing beacon dimmer: an LDR whose resistance changes between 161 kΩ (dark) and 0.8 kΩ (bright) forms a divider with a 20 kΩ resistor across 9 V (ideal). What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 161 + 20 = 181 kΩ, so I_dark = 9 / 181000 = 4.97 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.994 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 9 × 20 / (0.8 + 20) = 8.65 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.994 V.

items.stem: In a neonatal incubator thermal-alarm divider, an NTC thermistor (resistance decreases as temperature rises) has resistance 650 Ω at the operating point and sits in series with a 270 Ω fixed resistor across an ideal 9 V DC supply, as shown. What potential difference appears across the 650 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 270 + 650 = 920 Ω. Current I = 9 / 920 = 9.78 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 9 × 650 / 920 = 6.36 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0622 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 6.36 V.

items.stem: An NTC thermistor R_1 (resistance decreases with rising temperature) sits in series with a 700 Ω resistor across an ideal 8 V source in a lithium-ion pack over-temperature cutoff, as shown. When an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 3.00 V, what is the resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 700 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 8 − 3.00 = 5.00 V. Current I = 5.00 / 700 = 7.14 × 10⁻³ A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 3.00 / 7.14 × 10⁻³ = 420 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 5.00 V to find I = 7.14 × 10⁻³ A and R_1 = 420 Ω.

items.stem: The divider stage of an engine-coolant sensing bridge wires a 770 Ω reference resistor in series with an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient; 530 Ω at the test temperature) across an ideal 6 V source. What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 530 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 770 + 530 = 1300 Ω. Current I = 6 / 1300 = 4.62 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 6 × 530 / 1300 = 2.45 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0113 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.0113 W.

items.stem: In the 3D-printer hot-end thermistor loop diagram, R_1 is an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) wired in series with a 400 Ω precision resistor across an ideal 15 V supply. At an operating point where the p.d. across R_1 is 3.00 V, calculate R_1.
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 400 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 15 − 3.00 = 12.0 V. Current I = 12.0 / 400 = 0.0300 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 3.00 / 0.0300 = 100 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 12.0 V to find I = 0.0300 A and R_1 = 100 Ω.

items.stem: During steady-state calibration of a fermentation vat temperature regulator, an ideal 6 V cell drives a 430 Ω resistor in series with a 950 Ω NTC thermistor (whose resistance falls with increasing temperature). What potential difference appears across the 950 Ω NTC thermistor?

items.stem: Monitoring a quartz-crystal oven controller driven by an ideal 24 V cell, a technician records 9.00 V on an ideal voltmeter across NTC thermistor R_1 (whose resistance drops when warmed) in series with 1200 Ω. What is R_1?

items.stem: Within a vaccine cold-chain data-logger probe, a 270 Ω resistor and an NTC thermistor R_1 (negative temperature coefficient) share an ideal 15 V rail; given 6.00 V across R_1, find R_1's resistance.
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 270 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 15 − 6.00 = 9.00 V. Current I = 9.00 / 270 = 0.0333 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 6.00 / 0.0333 = 180 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 9.00 V to find I = 0.0333 A and R_1 = 180 Ω.

items.stem: In a server-blade heatsink thermal monitor, an NTC thermistor (resistance decreases as temperature rises) has resistance 1020 Ω at the operating point and sits in series with a 310 Ω fixed resistor across an ideal 12 V DC supply, as shown. What potential difference appears across the 1020 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 310 + 1020 = 1330 Ω. Current I = 12 / 1330 = 9.02 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 12 × 1020 / 1330 = 9.20 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0830 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 9.20 V.

items.stem: An NTC thermistor R_1 (resistance decreases with rising temperature) sits in series with a 900 Ω resistor across an ideal 18 V source in a water-bath thermostat calibration circuit, as shown. When an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 8.00 V, what is the resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 900 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 18 − 8.00 = 10.0 V. Current I = 10.0 / 900 = 0.0111 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 8.00 / 0.0111 = 720 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 10.0 V to find I = 0.0111 A and R_1 = 720 Ω.

items.stem: The divider stage of a PCR thermal-cycler block sensor wires a 640 Ω reference resistor in series with an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient; 550 Ω at the test temperature) across an ideal 10 V source. What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 550 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 640 + 550 = 1190 Ω. Current I = 10 / 1190 = 8.40 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 10 × 550 / 1190 = 4.62 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0388 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.0388 W.

items.stem: An ideal 10 V rail powers a blood-warmer safety cutoff divider containing a 470 Ω series resistor and an NTC thermistor (resistance 330 Ω, decreasing when heated). What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 330 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 470 + 330 = 800 Ω. Current I = 10 / 800 = 0.0125 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 10 × 330 / 800 = 4.13 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0516 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.0516 W.

items.stem: A starter-solenoid test battery of emf 17.36 V and internal resistance 1.6 Ω is wired directly across a 4 Ω external resistor, as shown. What is the terminal potential difference across the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 17.36 / (4 + 1.6) = 3.10 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 17.36 − (3.10)(1.6) = 12.4 V. External load power P = I² R = 38.4 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 12.4 V.

items.stem: In the schematic for a portable defibrillator battery module, a non-ideal cell (ε = 12.74 V, r = 1.3 Ω) supplies a single 8.5 Ω resistive load. What power is dissipated in the 8.5 Ω external load?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 12.74 / (8.5 + 1.3) = 1.30 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 12.74 − (1.30)(1.3) = 11.1 V. External load power P = I² R = 14.4 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 14.4 W.

items.stem: Load-testing a field transceiver LiFePO4 pack rated at emf 12.74 V with 2.2 Ω internal resistance, a technician connects a 16 Ω resistor across its terminals. What current is delivered by the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 12.74 / (16 + 2.2) = 0.700 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 12.74 − (0.700)(2.2) = 11.2 V. External load power P = I² R = 7.84 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 0.700 A.

items.stem: The circuit models a cordless drill high-drain battery as an ideal 6.5 V source in series with 1 Ω internal resistance driving a 4 Ω load. What is the terminal potential difference across the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 6.5 / (4 + 1) = 1.30 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 6.5 − (1.30)(1) = 5.20 V. External load power P = I² R = 6.76 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 5.20 V.

items.stem: Across the terminals of an emergency exit-lamp NiMH cell (emf 28.52 V, internal resistance 2.2 Ω), a 7 Ω resistor completes a closed loop. What power is dissipated in the 7 Ω external load?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 28.52 / (7 + 2.2) = 3.10 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 28.52 − (3.10)(2.2) = 21.7 V. External load power P = I² R = 67.3 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 67.3 W.

items.stem: When a 13 Ω load is connected to an underwater glider battery cell having ε = 30.02 V and r = 2.8 Ω as illustrated, what current is delivered by the battery?

items.stem: When a 7 Ω load is connected to a mine-rescue cap-lamp battery having ε = 13.13 V and r = 3.1 Ω as illustrated, what is the terminal potential difference across the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 13.13 / (7 + 3.1) = 1.30 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 13.13 − (1.30)(3.1) = 9.10 V. External load power P = I² R = 11.8 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 9.10 V.

items.stem: Refer to the diagram of a portable syringe-pump battery cell: internal resistance 1.6 Ω sits in series with emf 40.16 V across an external 23.5 Ω resistor. What power is dissipated in the 23.5 Ω external load?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 40.16 / (23.5 + 1.6) = 1.60 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 40.16 − (1.60)(1.6) = 37.6 V. External load power P = I² R = 60.2 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 60.2 W.

items.stem: A survey total-station battery pack of emf 34.88 V and internal resistance 1.3 Ω is wired directly across a 20.5 Ω external resistor, as shown. What current is delivered by the battery?
items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 34.88 / (20.5 + 1.3) = 1.60 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 34.88 − (1.60)(1.3) = 32.8 V. External load power P = I² R = 52.5 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 1.60 A.

items.stem: During a variable-resistor cell characterisation practical (modelled by source V with internal and load resistances R in series), terminal p.d. is 12.3 V at current 0.8 A and drops to 7.8 V when current increases to 2.8 A. What is the internal resistance of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (12.3 − 7.8)/(2.8 − 0.8) = 2.25 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 12.3 + (0.8)(2.25) = 14.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 2.25 Ω.

items.stem: In an MPPT solar-module bench test, ideal meters across a constant-r source record V_1 = 20.4 V when I_1 = 1.6 A, and V_2 = 13.8 V when I_2 = 4 A. What is the electromotive force (emf) of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (20.4 − 13.8)/(4 − 1.6) = 2.75 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 20.4 + (1.6)(2.75) = 24.8 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 24.8 V.

items.stem: Switching between two load settings in a fuel-cell polarisation-curve check (series loop shown) changes the current from 0.6 A to 5 A while terminal voltage falls from 30.8 V to 19.8 V. What is the internal resistance of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (30.8 − 19.8)/(5 − 0.6) = 2.50 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 30.8 + (0.6)(2.50) = 32.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 2.50 Ω.

items.stem: Two steady operating points are logged in an aircraft NiCd battery maintenance audit: (0.6 A, 23.4 V) and (3 A, 15 V). Assuming ohmic internal resistance, what is the electromotive force (emf) of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (23.4 − 15)/(3 − 0.6) = 3.50 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 23.4 + (0.6)(3.50) = 25.5 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 25.5 V.

items.stem: Two steady operating points are logged in an alkaline lantern-battery rheostat practical: (1 A, 13.8 V) and (3.4 A, 7.8 V). Assuming ohmic internal resistance, what is the internal resistance of the source?
items.workedSolution: Using V = ε − I r, internal resistance r = (V_1 − V_2)/(I_2 − I_1) = (13.8 − 7.8)/(3.4 − 1) = 2.50 Ω. Substituting back gives ε = V_1 + I_1 r = 13.8 + (1)(2.50) = 16.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: Solves simultaneous V = ε − I r equations to obtain 2.50 Ω.

items.stem: A battery of emf 16.8 V and internal resistance 3 Ω powers an off-grid cabin DC lighting and pump bus made of a 8 Ω series resistor and parallel 4 Ω and 12 Ω branches, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 20 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3.00 Ω, R_ext = 8 + 3.00 = 11.0 Ω, and R_tot = 11.0 + 3 = 14.0 Ω. Current I = 16.8 / 14.0 = 1.20 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 16.8 − (1.20)(3) = 13.2 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 317 J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 317 J.

items.stem: In the lunar rover heater and transceiver bus diagram, a non-ideal source (ε = 77 V, r = 1.5 Ω) feeds a 7 Ω line resistor ahead of parallel 45 Ω and 90 Ω loads. What is the battery's terminal potential difference during steady 15 s operation?

items.stem: Over a 40 s cycle of an electric-boat bilge and navigation circuit, a 25.2 V battery (1 Ω internal resistance) drives a 8 Ω resistor in series with parallel 15 Ω and 60 Ω resistors. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 40 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (15 × 60)/(15 + 60) = 12.0 Ω, R_ext = 8 + 12.0 = 20.0 Ω, and R_tot = 20.0 + 1 = 21.0 Ω. Current I = 25.2 / 21.0 = 1.20 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 25.2 − (1.20)(1) = 24.0 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 1.15 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 1.15 × 10³ J.

items.stem: A field-hospital DC distribution unit connects parallel 28 Ω and 84 Ω loads via a 2 Ω series resistor to a 26.5 V cell of internal resistance 3.5 Ω. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 40 s?

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 920 J.

items.stem: In the mine-shaft emergency beacon circuit diagram, a non-ideal source (ε = 11.2 V, r = 1 Ω) feeds a 4 Ω line resistor ahead of parallel 36 Ω and 12 Ω loads. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 90 s?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (36 × 12)/(36 + 12) = 9.00 Ω, R_ext = 4 + 9.00 = 13.0 Ω, and R_tot = 13.0 + 1 = 14.0 Ω. Current I = 11.2 / 14.0 = 0.800 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 11.2 − (0.800)(1) = 10.4 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 749 J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 749 J.

items.workedSolution: R_p = (24 × 48)/(24 + 48) = 16.0 Ω, R_ext = 5 + 16.0 = 21.0 Ω, and R_tot = 21.0 + 1 = 22.0 Ω. Current I = 26.4 / 22.0 = 1.20 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 26.4 − (1.20)(1) = 25.2 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 1.51 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 1.51 × 10³ J.

items.stem: A battery of emf 24 V and internal resistance 3 Ω powers a mobile blood-bank compressor DC loop made of a 7 Ω series resistor and parallel 14 Ω and 35 Ω branches, as shown. What is the battery's terminal potential difference during steady 15 s operation?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (14 × 35)/(14 + 35) = 10.0 Ω, R_ext = 7 + 10.0 = 17.0 Ω, and R_tot = 17.0 + 3 = 20.0 Ω. Current I = 24 / 20.0 = 1.20 A. Terminal p.d. V_term = 24 − (1.20)(3) = 20.4 V, and external energy E_ext = V_term I t = 367 J.

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 20.4 V.

items.stem: Over a 20 s cycle of a railway track-side battery cabinet, a 33 V battery (3 Ω internal resistance) drives a 9 Ω resistor in series with parallel 15 Ω and 30 Ω resistors. How much electrical energy is transferred to the external circuit over 20 s?

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 855 J.

items.stem: A cave-rescue repeater battery network connects parallel 21 Ω and 28 Ω loads via a 5 Ω series resistor to a 37 V cell of internal resistance 1.5 Ω. What is the battery's terminal potential difference during steady 50 s operation?

markScheme.criterion: Obtains 34.0 V.

items.stem: An immersive calorimetry heating coil uses a battery of emf 44 V and internal resistance 1 Ω wired across a 15 Ω heating load, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the 15 Ω load during 150 s?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 44 / (15 + 1) = 2.75 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 41.3 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 1.70 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 2.75 A and E_ext = I² R t = 1.70 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: In the cordless soldering-iron cartridge diagram, a cell (ε = 15.6 V, r = 0.7 Ω) supplies a 4.5 Ω external resistor steadily for 75 s. What total energy is delivered to the 4.5 Ω resistor?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 15.6 / (4.5 + 0.7) = 3.00 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 13.5 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 3.04 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 3.00 A and E_ext = I² R t = 3.04 × 10³ J.

items.stem: A hydrazine-line warming element uses a battery of emf 17.7 V and internal resistance 2.8 Ω wired across a 9 Ω heating load, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the 9 Ω load during 45 s?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 17.7 / (9 + 2.8) = 1.50 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 13.5 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 911 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 1.50 A and E_ext = I² R t = 911 J.

items.stem: A portable nebuliser heater element uses a battery of emf 52.75 V and internal resistance 1.6 Ω wired across a 19.5 Ω heating load, as shown. How much electrical energy is transferred to the 19.5 Ω load during 180 s?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 52.75 / (19.5 + 1.6) = 2.50 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 48.8 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 2.19 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 2.50 A and E_ext = I² R t = 2.19 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: In the laboratory oil-bath immersion coil diagram, a cell (ε = 22.65 V, r = 1.6 Ω) supplies a 13.5 Ω external resistor steadily for 20 s. What total energy is delivered to the 13.5 Ω resistor?
items.workedSolution: Current I = ε / (R + r) = 22.65 / (13.5 + 1.6) = 1.50 A. Potential difference across load V = I R = 20.3 V. Energy transferred to external load E = V I t = I² R t = 608 J.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 1.50 A and E_ext = I² R t = 608 J.

items.stem: In an observatory adaptive-optics cooling bus, a source of emf 25.8 V and internal resistance 0.9 Ω drives a 6 Ω resistor in series with parallel 9 Ω and 18 Ω branches for 50 s. What total electrical power is generated by the source emf?
items.workedSolution: R_p = (9 × 18)/(9 + 18) = 6.00 Ω; R_tot = 0.9 + 6 + 6.00 = 12.9 Ω. Source current I = 25.8 / 12.9 = 2.00 A. Total source power P_source = ε I = 25.8 × 2.00 = 51.6 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds I = 2.00 A and calculates P_source = ε I = 51.6 W.

items.stem: In a de-icing heater manifold on a weather mast, an ideal 20.4 V DC source drives a 11 Ω limiting resistor connected in series with parallel 18 Ω and 9 Ω resistors, as shown. What electrical power is dissipated in the 9 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (18 × 9)/(18 + 9) = 6.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 11 + 6.00 = 17.0 Ω. Supply current I = 20.4 / 17.0 = 1.20 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 1.20 × 6.00 = 7.20 V. Power in 9 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 9 = 5.76 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 7.20 V and calculates P = 5.76 W.

items.stem: While bench-testing a dual-zone incubator heating stage, an engineer wires a 17 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 15 Ω and 30 Ω resistors across an ideal 54 V supply. What potential difference develops across the parallel 15 Ω and 30 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (15 × 30)/(15 + 30) = 10.0 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 54 × 10.0 / (17 + 10.0) = 20.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 10.0 Ω and finds V_p = 20.0 V.

items.stem: An ideal 81 V power unit energises a submersible ROV auxiliary power bus made from a 15 Ω series element followed by 21 Ω and 28 Ω resistors in parallel, as illustrated. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (21 × 28)/(21 + 28) = 12.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 15 + 12.0 = 27.0 Ω. Supply current I = 81 / 27.0 = 3.00 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 15 Ω with R_p = 12.0 Ω to obtain I = 3.00 A.

items.stem: Parallel resistors of 18 Ω and 9 Ω inside a precision optical-table thermal stabiliser receive current through a 8 Ω series resistor from an ideal 49 V cell. What electrical power is dissipated in the 9 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (18 × 9)/(18 + 9) = 6.00 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 8 + 6.00 = 14.0 Ω. Supply current I = 49 / 14.0 = 3.50 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 3.50 × 6.00 = 21.0 V. Power in 9 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 9 = 49.0 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 21.0 V and calculates P = 49.0 W.

items.stem: A greenhouse misting-valve controller operates from an ideal 69.6 V rail; current traverses a 17 Ω ballast resistor before splitting across 20 Ω and 30 Ω parallel arms. What potential difference develops across the parallel 20 Ω and 30 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (20 × 30)/(20 + 30) = 12.0 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 69.6 × 12.0 / (17 + 12.0) = 28.8 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 12.0 Ω and finds V_p = 28.8 V.

items.stem: Examine the circuit for a vacuum-chamber bakeout resistor assembly, where a 9 Ω resistor stands in series with parallel 30 Ω and 60 Ω branches across an ideal 23.2 V source. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (30 × 60)/(30 + 60) = 20.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 9 + 20.0 = 29.0 Ω. Supply current I = 23.2 / 29.0 = 0.800 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 9 Ω with R_p = 20.0 Ω to obtain I = 0.800 A.

items.stem: In a traction-motor dynamic braking test bank, an ideal 52.8 V DC source drives a 13 Ω limiting resistor connected in series with parallel 30 Ω and 60 Ω resistors, as shown. What electrical power is dissipated in the 60 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (30 × 60)/(30 + 60) = 20.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 13 + 20.0 = 33.0 Ω. Supply current I = 52.8 / 33.0 = 1.60 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 1.60 × 20.0 = 32.0 V. Power in 60 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 60 = 17.1 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 32.0 V and calculates P = 17.1 W.

items.stem: While bench-testing a balloon telemetry heater loop, an engineer wires a 8 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 18 Ω and 9 Ω resistors across an ideal 28 V supply. What potential difference develops across the parallel 18 Ω and 9 Ω section?
items.workedSolution: Parallel resistance R_p = (18 × 9)/(18 + 9) = 6.00 Ω. By potential division, V_p = 28 × 6.00 / (8 + 6.00) = 12.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reduces parallel branches to 6.00 Ω and finds V_p = 12.0 V.

items.stem: An ideal 65 V power unit energises an industrial kiln damper actuator network made from a 6 Ω series element followed by 30 Ω and 60 Ω resistors in parallel, as illustrated. What current is drawn from the DC supply?
items.workedSolution: Equivalent parallel resistance R_p = (30 × 60)/(30 + 60) = 20.0 Ω. Total circuit resistance R_tot = 6 + 20.0 = 26.0 Ω. Supply current I = 65 / 26.0 = 2.50 A.

markScheme.criterion: Combines 6 Ω with R_p = 20.0 Ω to obtain I = 2.50 A.

items.stem: Parallel resistors of 21 Ω and 28 Ω inside a cryogenic transfer-line warm-up harness receive current through a 11 Ω series resistor from an ideal 36.8 V cell. What electrical power is dissipated in the 28 Ω parallel resistor?
items.workedSolution: Parallel equivalent R_p = (21 × 28)/(21 + 28) = 12.0 Ω. Total resistance R_tot = 11 + 12.0 = 23.0 Ω. Supply current I = 36.8 / 23.0 = 1.60 A. Parallel p.d. V_p = 1.60 × 12.0 = 19.2 V. Power in 28 Ω resistor P = V_p² / 28 = 13.2 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds V_p = 19.2 V and calculates P = 13.2 W.

items.stem: An automatic street-lamp twilight switch uses an ideal 15 V DC supply, an LDR, and a 2 kΩ fixed resistor wired as shown, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. The LDR resistance is 105 kΩ in darkness and 1 kΩ in bright light. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 105 + 2 = 107 kΩ, so I_dark = 15 / 107000 = 1.40 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.280 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 15 × 2 / (1 + 2) = 10.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 2 kΩ resistor to obtain 10.0 V.

items.stem: In the greenhouse shade-curtain controller diagram, an LDR (68 kΩ dark; 0.5 kΩ bright) sits in series with a 4 kΩ resistor across an ideal 12 V cell while ideal voltmeter Vout monitors the 4 kΩ resistor. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 68 + 4 = 72 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 72000 = 1.67 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 0.667 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 4 / (0.5 + 4) = 10.7 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 4 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.667 V.

items.stem: Testing a museum light-exposure alarm circuit supplied at 12 V (ideal), illumination lowers the LDR resistance from 171 kΩ in darkness to 1.2 kΩ in bright light; Vout is measured across the series 10 kΩ resistor. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 171 + 10 = 181 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 181000 = 6.63 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.663 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 10 / (1.2 + 10) = 10.7 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 10 kΩ resistor to obtain 6.63 × 10⁻⁵ A.

items.stem: The sensing stage of a photographic darkroom door interlock connects an LDR (116 kΩ in darkness, 0.5 kΩ when brightly lit) and a 20 kΩ resistor across an ideal 15 V source, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 116 + 20 = 136 kΩ, so I_dark = 15 / 136000 = 1.10 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 2.21 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 15 × 20 / (0.5 + 20) = 14.6 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 14.6 V.

items.stem: An ideal 15 V rail powers a solar tracker dusk-detection stage comprising an LDR (167 kΩ dark, 3.5 kΩ bright) in series with a 10 kΩ output resistor bridged by ideal voltmeter Vout. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 167 + 10 = 177 kΩ, so I_dark = 15 / 177000 = 8.47 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.847 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 15 × 10 / (3.5 + 10) = 11.1 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 10 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.847 V.

items.stem: Within a poultry-house lighting relay, an ideal voltmeter Vout spans a 6 kΩ resistor in series with an LDR (59 kΩ in darkness; 3.5 kΩ in bright daylight) across an ideal 6 V supply. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 59 + 6 = 65 kΩ, so I_dark = 6 / 65000 = 9.23 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.554 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 6 × 6 / (3.5 + 6) = 3.79 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 6 kΩ resistor to obtain 9.23 × 10⁻⁵ A.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a warehouse skylight dimming sensor: an LDR whose resistance changes between 66 kΩ (dark) and 3.5 kΩ (bright) forms a divider with a 2 kΩ resistor across 15 V (ideal). What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?

items.stem: A conveyor-belt optical package counter uses an ideal 5 V DC supply, an LDR, and a 20 kΩ fixed resistor wired as shown, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. The LDR resistance is 166 kΩ in darkness and 1.5 kΩ in bright light. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 166 + 20 = 186 kΩ, so I_dark = 5 / 186000 = 2.69 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.538 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 5 × 20 / (1.5 + 20) = 4.65 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 0.538 V.

items.stem: In the observatory dome-shutter safety sensor diagram, an LDR (94 kΩ dark; 1.5 kΩ bright) sits in series with a 20 kΩ resistor across an ideal 9 V cell while ideal voltmeter Vout monitors the 20 kΩ resistor. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 94 + 20 = 114 kΩ, so I_dark = 9 / 114000 = 7.89 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 1.58 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 9 × 20 / (1.5 + 20) = 8.37 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 7.89 × 10⁻⁵ A.

items.stem: Testing a meteorological sunshine-duration logger supplied at 6 V (ideal), illumination lowers the LDR resistance from 83 kΩ in darkness to 1.5 kΩ in bright light; Vout is measured across the series 15 kΩ resistor. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 83 + 15 = 98 kΩ, so I_dark = 6 / 98000 = 6.12 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.918 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 6 × 15 / (1.5 + 15) = 5.45 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 15 kΩ resistor to obtain 5.45 V.

items.stem: The sensing stage of a stairwell dusk-to-dawn LED trigger connects an LDR (91 kΩ in darkness, 1.2 kΩ when brightly lit) and a 20 kΩ resistor across an ideal 15 V source, with ideal voltmeter Vout across the fixed resistor. What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 91 + 20 = 111 kΩ, so I_dark = 15 / 111000 = 1.35 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 2.70 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 15 × 20 / (1.2 + 20) = 14.2 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 20 kΩ resistor to obtain 2.70 V.

items.stem: An ideal 24 V rail powers a highway tunnel entrance luminance monitor comprising an LDR (43 kΩ dark, 1.2 kΩ bright) in series with a 15 kΩ output resistor bridged by ideal voltmeter Vout. What current flows through the potential divider in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 43 + 15 = 58 kΩ, so I_dark = 24 / 58000 = 4.14 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 6.21 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 24 × 15 / (1.2 + 15) = 22.2 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 15 kΩ resistor to obtain 4.14 × 10⁻⁴ A.

items.stem: Within an aquarium photoperiod timer sensor, an ideal voltmeter Vout spans a 8 kΩ resistor in series with an LDR (158 kΩ in darkness; 1 kΩ in bright daylight) across an ideal 12 V supply. What does the ideal voltmeter Vout read in bright illumination?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 158 + 8 = 166 kΩ, so I_dark = 12 / 166000 = 7.23 × 10⁻⁵ A and V_out(dark) = 0.578 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 12 × 8 / (1 + 8) = 10.7 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 8 kΩ resistor to obtain 10.7 V.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a railway level-crossing beacon dimmer: an LDR whose resistance changes between 48 kΩ (dark) and 1.2 kΩ (bright) forms a divider with a 12 kΩ resistor across 18 V (ideal). What is the reading on the ideal voltmeter Vout in darkness?
items.workedSolution: In darkness, R_tot = 48 + 12 = 60 kΩ, so I_dark = 18 / 60000 = 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ A and V_out(dark) = 3.60 V. In bright light, V_out(bright) = 18 × 12 / (1.2 + 12) = 16.4 V.

markScheme.criterion: Applies potential-divider analysis across the 12 kΩ resistor to obtain 3.60 V.

items.stem: In a neonatal incubator thermal-alarm divider, an NTC thermistor (resistance decreases as temperature rises) has resistance 340 Ω at the operating point and sits in series with a 290 Ω fixed resistor across an ideal 15 V DC supply, as shown. What potential difference appears across the 340 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 290 + 340 = 630 Ω. Current I = 15 / 630 = 0.0238 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 15 × 340 / 630 = 8.10 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.193 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 8.10 V.

items.stem: An NTC thermistor R_1 (resistance decreases with rising temperature) sits in series with a 1080 Ω resistor across an ideal 33 V source in a lithium-ion pack over-temperature cutoff, as shown. When an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 15.0 V, what is the resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 1080 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 33 − 15.0 = 18.0 V. Current I = 18.0 / 1080 = 0.0167 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 15.0 / 0.0167 = 900 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 18.0 V to find I = 0.0167 A and R_1 = 900 Ω.

items.stem: The divider stage of an engine-coolant sensing bridge wires a 450 Ω reference resistor in series with an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient; 490 Ω at the test temperature) across an ideal 9 V source. What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 490 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 450 + 490 = 940 Ω. Current I = 9 / 940 = 9.57 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 9 × 490 / 940 = 4.69 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0449 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.0449 W.

items.stem: In the 3D-printer hot-end thermistor loop diagram, R_1 is an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) wired in series with a 540 Ω precision resistor across an ideal 16 V supply. At an operating point where the p.d. across R_1 is 10.0 V, calculate R_1.
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 540 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 16 − 10.0 = 6.00 V. Current I = 6.00 / 540 = 0.0111 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 10.0 / 0.0111 = 900 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 6.00 V to find I = 0.0111 A and R_1 = 900 Ω.

items.stem: During steady-state calibration of a fermentation vat temperature regulator, an ideal 12 V cell drives a 820 Ω resistor in series with a 330 Ω NTC thermistor (whose resistance falls with increasing temperature). What potential difference appears across the 330 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 820 + 330 = 1150 Ω. Current I = 12 / 1150 = 0.0104 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 12 × 330 / 1150 = 3.44 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0359 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 3.44 V.

items.stem: Monitoring a quartz-crystal oven controller driven by an ideal 15 V cell, a technician records 6.00 V on an ideal voltmeter across NTC thermistor R_1 (whose resistance drops when warmed) in series with 390 Ω. What is R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 390 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 15 − 6.00 = 9.00 V. Current I = 9.00 / 390 = 0.0231 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 6.00 / 0.0231 = 260 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 9.00 V to find I = 0.0231 A and R_1 = 260 Ω.

items.stem: An ideal 5 V rail powers an espresso boiler thermal-feedback divider containing a 750 Ω series resistor and an NTC thermistor (resistance 870 Ω, decreasing when heated). What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 870 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 750 + 870 = 1620 Ω. Current I = 5 / 1620 = 3.09 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 5 × 870 / 1620 = 2.69 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 8.29 × 10⁻³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 8.29 × 10⁻³ W.

items.stem: Within a vaccine cold-chain data-logger probe, a 420 Ω resistor and an NTC thermistor R_1 (negative temperature coefficient) share an ideal 9 V rail; given 3.00 V across R_1, find R_1's resistance.
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 420 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 9 − 3.00 = 6.00 V. Current I = 6.00 / 420 = 0.0143 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 3.00 / 0.0143 = 210 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 6.00 V to find I = 0.0143 A and R_1 = 210 Ω.

items.stem: An NTC thermistor R_1 (resistance decreases with rising temperature) sits in series with a 760 Ω resistor across an ideal 10 V source in a water-bath thermostat calibration circuit, as shown. When an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 2.00 V, what is the resistance of R_1?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference across the 760 Ω fixed resistor is V_s − V_NTC = 10 − 2.00 = 8.00 V. Current I = 8.00 / 760 = 0.0105 A. Hence R_1 = V_NTC / I = 2.00 / 0.0105 = 190 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V_fixed = 8.00 V to find I = 0.0105 A and R_1 = 190 Ω.

items.stem: The divider stage of a PCR thermal-cycler block sensor wires a 440 Ω reference resistor in series with an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient; 1130 Ω at the test temperature) across an ideal 5 V source. What is the self-heating electrical power dissipated in the 1130 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 440 + 1130 = 1570 Ω. Current I = 5 / 1570 = 3.18 × 10⁻³ A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 5 × 1130 / 1570 = 3.60 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0115 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 0.0115 W.

items.stem: In the induction-cooktop pan-temperature sensor diagram, R_1 is an NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) wired in series with a 400 Ω precision resistor across an ideal 24 V supply. At an operating point where the p.d. across R_1 is 18.0 V, calculate R_1.

items.stem: During steady-state calibration of a wind-turbine gearbox oil-temperature probe, an ideal 15 V cell drives a 660 Ω resistor in series with a 280 Ω NTC thermistor (whose resistance falls with increasing temperature). What potential difference appears across the 280 Ω NTC thermistor?
items.workedSolution: Total series resistance R_tot = 660 + 280 = 940 Ω. Current I = 15 / 940 = 0.0160 A. Potential difference across the NTC thermistor V_NTC = 15 × 280 / 940 = 4.47 V, and self-heating power P_NTC = I² R_NTC = 0.0713 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates series NTC potential divider to obtain 4.47 V.

items.workedSolution: Using ε = I(R + r): I = 36.89 / (8.5 + 3.4) = 3.10 A. Terminal p.d. V = ε − I r = 36.89 − (3.10)(3.4) = 26.4 V. External load power P = I² R = 81.7 W.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ε = I(R + r) to obtain 26.4 V.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 9.00 Ω and adds 6 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 15.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 1.60 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 14.4 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 12.
Obtains P = 17.3 W.

items.stem: Refer to the schematic of a marine radar waveguide dryer circuit: an ideal 37.5 V source drives a 9 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 18 Ω and 9 Ω resistors.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 6.00 Ω and adds 9 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 15.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 2.50 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 15.0 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 18.
Obtains P = 12.5 W.

Obtains V_p = 45.0 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 60.
Obtains P = 33.8 W.

items.stem: The resistive network of a geothermal logger downhole heater places 36 Ω and 12 Ω elements in parallel, fed via a 7 Ω series ballast from an ideal 12.8 V cell.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 9.00 Ω and adds 7 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 16.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 0.800 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 7.20 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 12.
Obtains P = 4.32 W.

Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 40.
Obtains P = 57.6 W.

items.stem: Across an ideal 6 V DC terminal pair in an automated venetian-blind lux sensor, an LDR of dark resistance 31 kΩ and bright-light resistance 1 kΩ sits in series with a 15 kΩ resistor spanned by ideal voltmeter Vout.

parts.prompt: Calculate the internal resistance of the source.
Determine the electromotive force (emf) of the source.

items.stem: To find ε and r in a portable generator exciter-battery test, two steady operating states are measured on the series circuit shown: I_1 = 1.6 A at V_1 = 29 V, and I_2 = 5.6 A at V_2 = 15 V.

markScheme.criterion: Equates internal resistance to (V_1 − V_2) / (I_2 − I_1).
Obtains r = 3.50 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + I r.
Obtains ε = 34.6 V.

items.stem: Across the linear DC source in a railways track-circuit cell audit (series model shown), stepping load current from 0.6 A up to 4.6 A causes terminal voltage to sag from 28.2 V to 16.2 V.

markScheme.criterion: Equates internal resistance to (V_1 − V_2) / (I_2 − I_1).
Obtains r = 3.00 Ω.
Substitutes r into ε = V + I r.
Obtains ε = 30.0 V.

items.stem: The diagram depicts a desert solar-kiosk night battery bus powered for 20 s by a non-ideal cell (ε = 22.8 V, r = 2 Ω) connected to 5 Ω in series with 21 Ω ∥ 28 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_ext = 17.0 Ω and adds 2 Ω internal resistance.
Obtains I = 1.20 A.
Applies V_term = ε − I r or I R_ext.
Obtains V_term = 20.4 V.
Uses E_ext = V_term I × 20.
Obtains E_ext = 490 J.

items.stem: Refer to a subsea benthic-lander battery harness shown: a 33.75 V source with 3.5 Ω internal resistance delivers current for 15 s through a 7 Ω resistor to parallel 20 Ω and 30 Ω arms.

markScheme.criterion: Finds R_ext = 19.0 Ω and adds 3.5 Ω internal resistance.
Obtains I = 1.50 A.
Applies V_term = ε − I r or I R_ext.
Obtains V_term = 28.5 V.
Uses E_ext = V_term I × 15.
Obtains E_ext = 641 J.

items.stem: To regulate heating in a cleanroom airlock interlock load bank, engineers connect parallel 45 Ω and 90 Ω resistors in series with a 13 Ω drop resistor across an ideal 150.5 V source.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 30.0 Ω and adds 13 Ω.

Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 90.
Obtains P = 123 W.

items.stem: During commissioning of a microplate reader warm-up stage, an ideal 27.2 V supply feeds a 9 Ω main-branch resistor followed by parallel 12 Ω and 24 Ω resistive loads.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 8.00 Ω and adds 9 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 17.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 1.60 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 12.8 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 12.
Obtains P = 13.7 W.

items.stem: The resistive network of a geothermal logger downhole heater places 12 Ω and 24 Ω elements in parallel, fed via a 9 Ω series ballast from an ideal 59.5 V cell.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 8.00 Ω and adds 9 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 17.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 3.50 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 28.0 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 24.
Obtains P = 32.7 W.

Obtains V_p = 19.2 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 20.
Obtains P = 18.4 W.

items.stem: Across an ideal 18 V DC terminal pair in an automated venetian-blind lux sensor, an LDR of dark resistance 46 kΩ and bright-light resistance 1 kΩ sits in series with a 10 kΩ resistor spanned by ideal voltmeter Vout.

markScheme.criterion: Converts kΩ to Ω and sums 46 kΩ + 10 kΩ.
Obtains I_dark = 3.21 × 10⁻⁴ A.
Multiplies I_dark by R_fixed or applies divider formula.
Obtains V_out(dark) = 3.21 V.
Uses bright LDR resistance 1 kΩ in potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_out(bright) = 16.4 V.

items.stem: Within an autoclave chamber temperature divider, series elements of 300 Ω and NTC thermistor R_1 (resistance drops as temperature rises) are energised by an ideal 18 V source; the potential difference across R_1 is 6.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts 6.00 V from 18 V to find p.d. across 300 Ω.
Obtains I = 0.0400 A.
Divides V_NTC by the series current from (a).
Obtains R_1 = 150 Ω.
Uses P = V I or I² R_1.
Obtains P = 0.240 W.

items.stem: In an HVAC supply-duct air-temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor R_1 (negative temperature coefficient: resistance decreases as temperature increases) is wired in series with a 1440 Ω resistor across an ideal 27 V DC source, as shown. At the test temperature, an ideal voltmeter across R_1 reads 9.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts 9.00 V from 27 V to find p.d. across 1440 Ω.
Obtains I = 0.0125 A.
Divides V_NTC by the series current from (a).
Obtains R_1 = 720 Ω.
Uses P = V I or I² R_1.
Obtains P = 0.113 W.

items.stem: In a railway point-heater distribution box, parallel resistors of resistance 12 Ω and 24 Ω are wired in series with a 3 Ω resistor across an ideal 13.2 V DC terminal pair.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates parallel resistance R_p = 8.00 Ω and adds 3 Ω.
Obtains R_tot = 11.0 Ω.
Finds supply current 1.20 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 9.60 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 24.
Obtains P = 3.84 W.

Finds supply current 2.50 A or applies potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_p = 30.0 V.
Substitutes V_p into P = V_p² / 18.
Obtains P = 50.0 W.

items.stem: Across an ideal 5 V DC terminal pair in an automated venetian-blind lux sensor, an LDR of dark resistance 118 kΩ and bright-light resistance 0.5 kΩ sits in series with a 3 kΩ resistor spanned by ideal voltmeter Vout.

markScheme.criterion: Converts kΩ to Ω and sums 118 kΩ + 3 kΩ.
Obtains I_dark = 4.13 × 10⁻⁵ A.
Multiplies I_dark by R_fixed or applies divider formula.
Obtains V_out(dark) = 0.124 V.
Uses bright LDR resistance 0.5 kΩ in potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_out(bright) = 4.29 V.

Determine the voltmeter reading Vout in darkness.
Calculate the voltmeter reading Vout when the LDR is exposed to bright light.

items.stem: Examine the camera exposure-meter bridge arm circuit shown: an ideal 5 V cell drives an LDR (124 kΩ dark; 2.5 kΩ bright) and a 20 kΩ fixed resistor across which ideal voltmeter Vout is connected.

markScheme.criterion: Converts kΩ to Ω and sums 124 kΩ + 20 kΩ.
Obtains I_dark = 3.47 × 10⁻⁵ A.
Multiplies I_dark by R_fixed or applies divider formula.
Obtains V_out(dark) = 0.694 V.
Uses bright LDR resistance 2.5 kΩ in potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_out(bright) = 4.44 V.

items.stem: A cleanroom UV-lamp verification sensor connects an LDR in series with a 8 kΩ fixed resistor across an ideal 12 V DC source, with ideal voltmeter Vout connected across the 8 kΩ resistor as shown. The LDR resistance is 102 kΩ in darkness and 0.5 kΩ in bright light.

markScheme.criterion: Converts kΩ to Ω and sums 102 kΩ + 8 kΩ.
Obtains I_dark = 1.09 × 10⁻⁴ A.
Multiplies I_dark by R_fixed or applies divider formula.
Obtains V_out(dark) = 0.873 V.
Uses bright LDR resistance 0.5 kΩ in potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_out(bright) = 11.3 V.

items.stem: In the schematic for a heliostat cloud-cover trip divider, an ideal 18 V cell supplies a potential divider formed by an LDR (166 kΩ in darkness; 1.2 kΩ in bright light) and a 3 kΩ resistor monitored by ideal voltmeter Vout.

markScheme.criterion: Converts kΩ to Ω and sums 166 kΩ + 3 kΩ.
Obtains I_dark = 1.07 × 10⁻⁴ A.
Multiplies I_dark by R_fixed or applies divider formula.
Obtains V_out(dark) = 0.320 V.
Uses bright LDR resistance 1.2 kΩ in potential-divider ratio.
Obtains V_out(bright) = 12.9 V.

items.stem: An ideal voltmeter Vout measures the output across a 5 kΩ resistor in series with an LDR inside a botanical growth-cabinet lux monitor powered at 5 V (ideal); the LDR has resistance 34 kΩ in darkness and 2.5 kΩ under bright illumination.

markScheme.criterion: Converts kΩ to Ω and sums 34 kΩ + 5 kΩ.

items.stem: A pasteurisation-line temperature monitor pairs a 900 Ω reference resistor in series with an NTC thermistor R_1 (whose resistance falls when heated) across an ideal 14 V cell; an ideal voltmeter across R_1 registers 4.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts 4.00 V from 14 V to find p.d. across 900 Ω.

Uses P = V I or I² R_1.
Obtains P = 0.0444 W.
